### V-254256 · WN22-00-000190 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 outdated or unused accounts must be removed or disabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254256r1260022_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000118-GPOS-00060 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000017 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (3) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (3) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (3) |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's outdated or unused accounts must be removed or disabled.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -UsersOnly -TimeSpan 35.00:00:00
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-LocalUser | Where-Object { $_.Enabled -and $_.LastLogon -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-35) } | Select-Object Name, LastLogon
```

Expected: No enabled accounts listed (accounts that never logged on show an empty LastLogon).

**How it works:** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Open "Windows PowerShell".

Domain Controllers:

Enter "Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -UsersOnly -TimeSpan 35.00:00:00"

This will return accounts that have not been logged on to for 35 days, along with various attributes such as the Enabled status and LastLogonDate.

Member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems:

Copy or enter the lines below to the PowerShell window and enter. (Entering twice may be required. Do not include the quotes at the beginning and end of the query.)

"([ADSI]('WinNT://{0}' -f $env:COMPUTERNAME)).Children | Where { $_.SchemaClassName -eq 'user' } | ForEach {
 $user = ([ADSI]$_.Path)
 $lastLogin = $user.Properties.LastLogin.Value
 $enabled = ($user.Properties.UserFlags.Value -band 0x2) -ne 0x2
 if ($lastLogin -eq $null) {
 $lastLogin = 'Never'
 }
 Write-Host $user.Name $lastLogin $enabled
}"

This will return a list of local accounts with the account name, last logon, and if the account is enabled (True/False).
For example: User1 10/31/2025 5:49:56 AM True

Review the list of accounts returned by the above queries to determine the finding validity for each account reported.

Exclude the following accounts:

- Built-in administrator account (Renamed, SID ending in 500)
- Built-in guest account (Renamed, Disabled, SID ending in 501)
- Application accounts

If any enabled accounts have not been logged on to within the past 35 days, this is a finding.

Inactive accounts that have been reviewed and deemed to be required must be documented with the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Regularly review accounts to determine if they are still active. Remove or disable accounts that have not been used in the last 35 days.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Outdated or unused accounts provide penetration points that may go undetected. Inactive accounts must be deleted if no longer necessary or, if still required, disabled until needed.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000017**: Disable accounts when the accounts have been inactive for the organization-defined time-period.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (3) (d) · Rev 4: AC-2 (3) · Rev 3: AC-2 (3)

### V-254257 · WN22-00-000200 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 accounts must require passwords.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254257r958482_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000104-GPOS-00051 |
| Topic | PowerShell & Scripting Security |
| CCI | CCI-000764 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-2 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's accounts must require passwords.

**Why it matters:** PowerShell is a powerful tool for automating tasks on Windows, which also makes it a favorite of hackers. This rule makes the computer keep a detailed record of every PowerShell command that runs, like a CCTV camera pointed at the most powerful tool in the workshop.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-Aduser -Filter * -Properties Passwordnotrequired |FT Name, Passwordnotrequired, Enabled
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, configure these under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows PowerShell: 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging EnableScriptBlockLogging = 1) and 'Turn on PowerShell Transcription'. Logs go to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. Write transcripts to a protected, centrally collected location.

**Operational impact:** Script-block logs can be large and may capture secrets embedded in scripts. Size the PowerShell Operational log appropriately and restrict who can read it.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the password required status for enabled user accounts.

Open "PowerShell".

Domain Controllers:

Enter "Get-Aduser -Filter * -Properties Passwordnotrequired |FT Name, Passwordnotrequired, Enabled".

Exclude disabled accounts (e.g., DefaultAccount, Guest) and Trusted Domain Objects (TDOs).

If "Passwordnotrequired" is "True" or blank for any enabled user account, this is a finding.

Member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems:

Enter 'Get-CimInstance -Class Win32_Useraccount -Filter "PasswordRequired=False and LocalAccount=True" | FT Name, PasswordRequired, Disabled, LocalAccount'.

Exclude disabled accounts (e.g., DefaultAccount, Guest).

If any enabled user accounts are returned with a "PasswordRequired" status of "False", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure all enabled accounts to require passwords.

The password required flag can be set by entering the following on a command line: "Net user [username] /passwordreq:yes", substituting [username] with the name of the user account.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The lack of password protection enables anyone to gain access to the information system, which opens a backdoor opportunity for intruders to compromise the system as well as other resources. Accounts on a system must require passwords.

**Threat & control context:** PowerShell is the dominant 'living off the land' tool in Windows intrusions. Script Block Logging (event 4104) records de-obfuscated code as it executes, and Transcription records full session input and output. Together they provide high-fidelity detection content for AU-2/AU-12 and SI-4. Removing PowerShell 2.0 prevents downgrade attacks that bypass these logs and AMSI.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell; T1059.005 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic; T1562.003 Impair Defenses: Impair Command History Logging

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000764**: Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users and associate that unique identification with processes acting on behalf of those users.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 · Rev 4: IA-2 · Rev 3: IA-2

### V-254258 · WN22-00-000210 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 passwords must be configured to expire.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254258r1051089_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000076-GPOS-00044 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse |
| CCI | CCI-004066, CCI-000199 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (h) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's passwords must be configured to expire.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly | FT Name, PasswordNeverExpires, Enabled
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the password never expires status for enabled user accounts.

Open "PowerShell".

Domain Controllers:

Enter "Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly | FT Name, PasswordNeverExpires, Enabled".

Exclude application accounts, disabled accounts (e.g., DefaultAccount, Guest) and the krbtgt account.

If any enabled user accounts are returned with a "PasswordNeverExpires" status of "True", this is a finding.

Member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems:

Enter 'Get-CimInstance -Class Win32_Useraccount -Filter "PasswordExpires=False and LocalAccount=True" | FT Name, PasswordExpires, Disabled, LocalAccount'.

Exclude application accounts and disabled accounts (e.g., DefaultAccount, Guest).

If any enabled user accounts are returned with a "PasswordExpires" status of "False", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure all enabled user account passwords to expire.

Uncheck "Password never expires" for all enabled user accounts in Active Directory Users and Computers for domain accounts and Users in Computer Management for member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems. Document any exceptions with the  information system security officer (ISSO).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Passwords that do not expire or are reused increase the exposure of a password with greater probability of being discovered or cracked.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000199**: The information system enforces maximum password lifetime restrictions.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (d)

### V-254259 · WN22-00-000220 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 system files must be monitored for unauthorized changes.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254259r958794_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000363-GPOS-00150 |
| Topic | Software & File Integrity Verification |
| CCI | CCI-001744 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-3 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer files must be monitored for unauthorized changes.

**Why it matters:** This makes the computer check a digital "seal" on software before installing it, and keep a fingerprint of important files so it can notice if anyone changes them. It's like checking that a medicine bottle's safety seal is intact, and noticing straight away if someone has tampered with it.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, use WDAC/AppLocker for signature enforcement, 'sfc /verifyonly' for system file verification, and the enterprise FIM product.

**Operational impact:** AIDE reports every legitimate change too, so re-baseline after approved patching and keep the database read-only or off-host. Internal repositories must sign their packages, or clients will refuse them.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine whether the system is monitored for unauthorized changes to system files (e.g., *.exe, *.bat, *.com, *.cmd, and *.dll) against a baseline on a weekly basis.

If system files are not monitored for unauthorized changes, this is a finding.

An approved and properly configured solution will contain both a list of baselines that includes all system file locations and a file comparison task that is scheduled to run at least weekly.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Monitor the system for unauthorized changes to system files (e.g., *.exe, *.bat, *.com, *.cmd, and *.dll) against a baseline on a weekly basis. This can be done with the use of various monitoring tools.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Monitoring system files for changes against a baseline on a regular basis may help detect the possible introduction of malicious code on a system.

**Threat & control context:** Signature verification ensures only vendor-authentic software is installed (CM-14 signed components, SI-7 software and information integrity). File-integrity monitoring such as AIDE detects unauthorized modification of binaries and configuration after the fact (SI-7(1), CM-3(5)), catching rootkits, backdoored binaries and configuration drift. The value of FIM depends on protecting the baseline database off-host and acting on alerts.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1195 Supply Chain Compromise; T1554 Compromise Host Software Binary; T1014 Rootkit

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001744**: Implement organization-defined security responses automatically if baseline configurations are changed in an unauthorized manner.  
  Rev 5: CM-3 (5) · Rev 4: CM-3 (5) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254260 · WN22-00-000230 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 nonsystem-created file shares must limit access to groups that require it.

| Rule ID | `SV-254260r1137695_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's nonsystem-created file shares must limit access to groups that require it.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-SmbShare | Where-Object Special -eq $false | Get-SmbShareAccess
```

Expected: Only groups that need access are listed; no 'Everyone' with Full or Change access.

*CMD* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
net share
```

Expected: Review any non-default shares (ADMIN$, C$, IPC$, NETLOGON and SYSVOL are system-created).

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If only system-created shares such as "ADMIN$", "C$", and "IPC$" exist on the system, this is NA. (System-created shares will display a message that it has been shared for administrative purposes when "Properties" is selected.)

Run "Computer Management".

Navigate to System Tools >> Shared Folders >> Shares.

Right-click any nonsystem-created shares.

Select "Properties".

Select the "Share Permissions" tab.

If the file shares have not been configured to restrict permissions to the specific groups or accounts that require access, this is a finding.

Select the "Security" tab.

If the permissions have not been configured to restrict permissions to the specific groups or accounts that require access, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
If a nonsystem-created share is required on a system, configure the share and NTFS permissions to limit access to the specific groups or accounts that require it.

Remove any unnecessary nonsystem-created shares.
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Shares on a system provide network access. To prevent exposing sensitive information, where shares are necessary, permissions must be reconfigured to give the minimum access to accounts that require it.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-254261 · WN22-00-000240 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must have software certificate installation files removed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254261r1210262_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have software certificate installation files removed.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -Include *.p12, *.pfx -File -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object FullName
```

Expected: No results (other than approved, documented files).

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Search all drives for *.p12 and *.pfx files.

If any files with these extensions exist, this is a finding.

This does not apply to server-based applications that have a requirement for .p12 or .pfx certificate files. Some applications create files with extensions of .p12 or .pfx that are not certificate installation files. Removal of noncertificate installation files from systems is not required. These must be documented with the information system security officer (ISSO).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove any certificate installation files (*.p12 and *.pfx) found on a system.

Note: This does not apply to server-based applications that have a requirement for .p12 or .pfx certificate files.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Use of software certificates and their accompanying installation files for end users to access resources is less secure than the use of hardware-based certificates.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-254262 · WN22-00-000250 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 systems requiring data-at-rest protections must employ cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the information at rest.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254262r1210265_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000185-GPOS-00079 |
| Topic | Data-at-Rest Encryption |
| CCI | CCI-001199, CCI-002475, CCI-002476 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-28, SC-28 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-28 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer requiring data-at-rest protections must employ cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure and modification of the information at rest.

**Why it matters:** This scrambles everything stored on the computer's drive so it can only be read after the right key or PIN is entered at startup. If someone steals the laptop or pulls out the hard drive, all they get is gibberish. It's like keeping your documents in a locked safe instead of a cardboard box.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *FIPS 140*: A U.S. government standard for testing and approving encryption software.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
manage-bde -status
```

Expected: Every fixed volume shows 'Protection On' and 'Fully Encrypted'. Run elevated.

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-BitLockerVolume | Select-Object MountPoint, VolumeStatus, ProtectionStatus, KeyProtector
```

Expected: ProtectionStatus On and VolumeStatus FullyEncrypted for every fixed volume.

**How it works:** Windows uses BitLocker, controlled by Group Policy under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> BitLocker Drive Encryption (registry HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\FVE). Verify with 'manage-bde -status'. Escrow recovery keys to AD DS or Entra ID before enforcing PIN requirements.

**Operational impact:** Requiring a pre-boot PIN means unattended reboots (patch windows, remote power-cycles) stop at the PIN prompt unless Network Unlock is deployed. Plan key escrow and helpdesk recovery procedures before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify systems that require additional protections due to factors such as inadequate physical protection or sensitivity of the data employ encryption to protect the confidentiality and integrity of all information at rest.

Note: If there is a documented and approved reason to omit data-at-rest encryption at the operating system level, such as encryption provided by a hypervisor or a disk storage array in a virtualized environment, this requirement is not applicable.

If there is no evidence that persistent user-generated data and operating system-specific configuration data are encrypted, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure systems that require data-at-rest protections to employ encryption to protect the confidentiality and integrity of all persistent user-generated data and operating system-specific configuration data.

The encryption method implemented must use FIPS-compliant algorithms.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This requirement addresses protection of user-generated data as well as operating system-specific configuration data. Organizations may choose to employ different mechanisms to achieve confidentiality and integrity protections, as appropriate, in accordance with the security category and/or classification of the information.

Selection of a cryptographic mechanism is based on the need to protect the integrity of organizational information. The strength of the mechanism is commensurate with the security category and/or classification of the information. Organizations have the flexibility to either encrypt all information on storage devices (i.e., full disk encryption) or encrypt specific data structures (e.g., files, records, or fields).

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000185-GPOS-00079, SRG-OS-000404-GPOS-00183, SRG-OS-000405-GPOS-00184

**Threat & control context:** Full-volume encryption protects confidentiality when an adversary gains physical possession of storage, an attack path that bypasses every OS-level access control. Pre-boot authentication (TPM + PIN) defends against cold-boot, DMA and TPM-sniffing attacks that defeat TPM-only configurations. Maps primarily to SC-28 (Protection of Information at Rest). Assess key escrow and recovery procedures as well, because an unrecoverable key is an availability risk.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1005 Data from Local System; T1200 Hardware Additions; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001199**: Protects the confidentiality and/or integrity of organization-defined information at rest.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 · Rev 4: SC-28 · Rev 3: SC-28
- **CCI-002475**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized modification of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002476**: Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent unauthorized disclosure of organization-defined information at rest on organization-defined system components.  
  Rev 5: SC-28 (1) · Rev 4: SC-28 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254263 · WN22-00-000260 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must implement protection methods such as TLS, encrypted VPNs, or IPsec if the data owner has a strict requirement for ensuring data integrity and confidentiality is maintained at every step of the data transfer and handling process.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254263r958912_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000425-GPOS-00189 |
| Topic | Approved Cryptography (FIPS 140) |
| CCI | CCI-002420, CCI-002422 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-8 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-8 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must implement protection methods such as TLS, encrypted VPNs, or IPsec if the data owner has a strict requirement for ensuring data integrity and confidentiality is maintained at every step of the data transfer and handling process.

**Why it matters:** Encryption is how computers scramble information so eavesdroppers can't read it. Some older scrambling methods have been "cracked" and are no longer safe. This rule makes the computer use only methods the U.S. government has tested and approved, like requiring modern, certified locks instead of old ones that a locksmith can easily pick.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, 'System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing' (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\FIPSAlgorithmPolicy\Enabled) restricts Schannel and CNG to FIPS-approved algorithms. Related settings cover Kerberos encryption types and NTLM session security.

**Operational impact:** Enabling FIPS mode can break applications that use non-approved algorithms (MD5 for non-security checksums, older .NET code, legacy VPN or RDP clients). Test interoperating systems and line-of-business applications before rollout.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
If the data owner has a strict requirement for ensuring data integrity and confidentiality is maintained at every step of the data transfer and handling process, verify protection methods such as TLS, encrypted VPNs, or IPsec have been implemented.

If protection methods have not been implemented, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure protection methods such as TLS, encrypted VPNs, or IPsec when the data owner has a strict requirement for ensuring data integrity and confidentiality is maintained at every step of the data transfer and handling process.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Information can be either unintentionally or maliciously disclosed or modified during preparation for transmission, for example, during aggregation, at protocol transformation points, and during packing/unpacking. These unauthorized disclosures or modifications compromise the confidentiality or integrity of the information.

Ensuring the confidentiality of transmitted information requires the operating system to take measures in preparing information for transmission. This can be accomplished via access control and encryption.

Use of this requirement will be limited to situations where the data owner has a strict requirement for ensuring data integrity and confidentiality is maintained at every step of the data transfer and handling process. When transmitting data, operating systems need to support transmission protection mechanisms such as TLS, encrypted VPNs, or IPsec.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000425-GPOS-00189, SRG-OS-000426-GPOS-00190

**Threat & control context:** Federal systems must use FIPS 140-validated cryptographic modules (SC-13). Weak or legacy algorithms (MD5, SHA-1 MACs, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, DES/3DES, small DH groups) enable downgrade, decryption or forgery attacks against data in transit (SC-8, SC-8(1)). The control is only as strong as its weakest negotiated option, so assessors look at the full allowed list, not just the preferred algorithm. Note that FIPS mode validates the module, not the protocol configuration, so both must be checked.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1040 Network Sniffing; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1600 Weaken Encryption

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002420**: Maintain the confidentiality and/or integrity of information during preparation for transmission.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (2) · Rev 4: SC-8 (2) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-002422**: Maintain the confidentiality and/or integrity of information during reception.  
  Rev 5: SC-8 (2) · Rev 4: SC-8 (2) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254264 · WN22-00-000270 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must have the roles and features required by the system documented.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254264r1186389_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the roles and features required by the system documented.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object {$_. installstate -eq
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object Installed | Select-Object Name, DisplayName
```

Expected: Only roles and features documented as required for the server's function.

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Required roles and features will vary based on the function of the individual system.

Roles and features specifically required to be disabled per the STIG are identified in separate requirements.

If the organization has not documented the roles and features required for the system(s), this is a finding.

The PowerShell command "Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object {$_. installstate -eq "Installed"} | Format-List Displayname, Name, Featuretype" will list all roles and features with an "Installed" state.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Document the roles and features required for the system to operate. Uninstall any that are not required.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unnecessary roles and features increase the attack surface of a system. Limiting roles and features of a system to only those necessary reduces this potential. The standard installation option (previously called Server Core) further reduces this when selected at installation.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-254265 · WN22-00-000280 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must have a host-based firewall installed and enabled.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254265r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Host Firewall |
| CCI | CCI-000366, CCI-002080 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b, CA-3 (5) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have a host-based firewall installed and enabled.

**Why it matters:** A firewall is a gatekeeper that decides which network connections are allowed in and out of the computer. This rule makes sure the gatekeeper is switched on and turns away anything that isn't on the approved list, like a security guard who only lets in people with an appointment.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Firewall*: A filter that decides which network connections are allowed in or out.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction
```

Expected: Enabled True for Domain, Private and Public (or another DoD-approved firewall is installed).

**How it works:** On Windows, use Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security. Turn it on for the Domain, Private and Public profiles with inbound set to block by default. Scope management rules (RDP, WinRM, SMB) to the management subnets. Verify with 'Get-NetFirewallProfile' and 'Get-NetFirewallRule'.

**Operational impact:** An over-restrictive default can cut off management or application traffic. Make changes from the console, or stage them with a timed rollback ('firewall-cmd --timeout').

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine if a host-based firewall is installed and enabled on the system.

If a host-based firewall is not installed and enabled on the system, this is a finding.

The configuration requirements will be determined by the applicable firewall STIG.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Install and enable a host-based firewall on the system.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A firewall provides a line of defense against attack, allowing or blocking inbound and outbound connections based on a set of rules.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227, SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00232

**Threat & control context:** A host firewall enforces deny-by-default, allow-by-exception at the endpoint (SC-7(5)) and contains lateral movement even when the perimeter is breached or the host sits on a flat network. Exposed ports must match the system's PPSM registration (CM-7(1)). Remote-management exceptions should be scoped to authorized management hosts rather than 'any'. Check that the firewall service can't be stopped by non-administrators and that rule changes are audited.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.004 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify System Firewall; T1021 Remote Services; T1046 Network Service Discovery

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b
- **CCI-002080**: The organization employs either an allow-all, deny-by-exception or a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy for allowing organization-defined information systems to connect to external information systems.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: CA-3 (5) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254267 · WN22-00-000300 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must automatically remove or disable temporary user accounts after 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254267r1256686_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000002-GPOS-00002 |
| Topic | Account Lifecycle Management |
| CCI | CCI-000016 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically remove or disable temporary user accounts after 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** Every person should have their own account, and accounts that nobody is using (people who left, temporary contractors, test accounts) should be turned off. Forgotten accounts are like old keys still floating around after someone moves out. You never know who might use them.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Search-ADAccount -AccountExpiring | FT Name, AccountExpirationDate
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Before you automatically disable inactive accounts, confirm that service, break-glass and seasonal-user accounts are inventoried and either exempted with documentation or monitored.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review temporary user accounts for expiration dates.

Determine if temporary user accounts are used and identify any that exist. If none exist, this is NA.

Domain Controllers:

Open "PowerShell".

Enter "Search-ADAccount -AccountExpiring | FT Name, AccountExpirationDate".

If "AccountExpirationDate" has not been defined within 72 hours for any temporary user account, this is a finding.

Member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems:

Open "Command Prompt".

Run "Net user [username]", where [username] is the name of the temporary user account.

If "Account expires" has not been defined within 72 hours for any temporary user account, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure temporary user accounts to automatically expire within 72 hours.

Domain accounts can be configured with an account expiration date, under "Account" properties.

Local accounts can be configured to expire with the command "Net user [username] /expires:[mm/dd/yyyy]", where [username] is the name of the temporary user account.

Delete any temporary user accounts that are no longer necessary.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** If temporary user accounts remain active when no longer needed or for an excessive period, these accounts may be used to gain unauthorized access. To mitigate this risk, automated termination of all temporary accounts must be set upon account creation.

Temporary accounts are established as part of normal account activation procedures when there is a need for short-term accounts without the demand for immediacy in account activation.

If temporary accounts are used, the operating system must be configured to automatically terminate these types of accounts after a DoW-defined time period of 72 hours.

To address access requirements, many operating systems may be integrated with enterprise-level authentication/access mechanisms that meet or exceed access control policy requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Dormant, orphaned and shared accounts are prime persistence and initial-access vectors because nobody notices their use. AC-2 (Account Management) and its enhancements (AC-2(2) temporary/emergency account removal, AC-2(3) disable inactive accounts) require automated lifecycle enforcement. IA-2 and IA-4 require unique identifiers so actions can be attributed to individuals. Assessors typically sample accounts against an authoritative roster.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000016**: Automatically remove or disable temporary and emergency accounts after an organization-defined time-period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

---

### V-254268 · WN22-00-000310 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after the crisis is resolved or within 72 hours.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254268r958508_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000123-GPOS-00064 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-001682 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-2 (2) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-2 (2) |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after the crisis is resolved or within 72 hours.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Search-ADAccount -AccountExpiring | FT Name, AccountExpirationDate
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine if emergency administrator accounts are used and identify any that exist. If none exist, this is NA.

If emergency administrator accounts cannot be configured with an expiration date due to an ongoing crisis, the accounts must be disabled or removed when the crisis is resolved.

If emergency administrator accounts have not been configured with an expiration date or have not been disabled or removed following the resolution of a crisis, this is a finding.

Domain Controllers:

Open "PowerShell".

Enter "Search-ADAccount -AccountExpiring | FT Name, AccountExpirationDate".

If "AccountExpirationDate" has been defined and is not within 72 hours for an emergency administrator account, this is a finding.

Member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems:

Open "Command Prompt".

Run "Net user [username]", where [username] is the name of the emergency account.

If "Account expires" has been defined and is not within 72 hours for an emergency administrator account, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove emergency administrator accounts after a crisis has been resolved or configure the accounts to automatically expire within 72 hours.

Domain accounts can be configured with an account expiration date, under "Account" properties.

Local accounts can be configured to expire with the command "Net user [username] /expires:[mm/dd/yyyy]", where [username] is the name of the temporary user account.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Emergency administrator accounts are privileged accounts established in response to crisis situations where the need for rapid account activation is required. Therefore, emergency account activation may bypass normal account authorization processes. If these accounts are automatically disabled, system maintenance during emergencies may not be possible, thus adversely affecting system availability.

Emergency administrator accounts are different from infrequently used accounts (i.e., local logon accounts used by system administrators when network or normal logon/access is not available). Infrequently used accounts are not subject to automatic termination dates. Emergency accounts are accounts created in response to crisis situations, usually for use by maintenance personnel. The automatic expiration or disabling time period may be extended as needed until the crisis is resolved; however, it must not be extended indefinitely. A permanent account must be established for privileged users who need long-term maintenance accounts.

To address access requirements, many operating systems can be integrated with enterprise-level authentication/access mechanisms that meet or exceed access control policy requirements.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001682**: Automatically remove or disable emergency accounts after an organization-defined time period for each type of account.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (2) · Rev 4: AC-2 (2) · Rev 3: AC-2 (2)

### V-254269 · WN22-00-000320 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must not have the Fax Server role installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254269r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Windows feature |

### V-254275 · WN22-00-000380 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must not the Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254275r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Windows feature |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not the Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol installed.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *SMB*: Server Message Block: the protocol Windows uses for file and printer sharing.
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feature | Windows feature | FS-SMB1 | Removed |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-WindowsFeature -Name FS-SMB1
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-WindowsFeature | Where-Object { $_.DisplayName -eq 'FS-SMB1' -or $_.Name -eq 'FS-SMB1' } | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, InstallState
```

Expected: InstallState must be 'Available' or 'Removed' (not 'Installed').

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Different methods are available to disable SMBv1 on Windows Server 2022. This is the preferred method, however if WN22-00-000390 and WN22-00-000400 are configured, this is NA.

Open "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter "Get-WindowsFeature -Name FS-SMB1".

If "Installed State" is "Installed", this is a finding.

An Installed State of "Available" or "Removed" is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Uninstall the SMBv1 protocol.

Open "Windows PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter "Uninstall-WindowsFeature -Name FS-SMB1 -Restart".
(Omit the Restart parameter if an immediate restart of the system cannot be done.)

Alternately:

Start "Server Manager".

Select the server with the feature.

Scroll down to "ROLES AND FEATURES" in the right pane.

Select "Remove Roles and Features" from the drop-down "TASKS" list.

Select the appropriate server on the "Server Selection" page and click "Next".

Deselect "SMB 1.0/CIFS File Sharing Support" on the "Features" page.

Click "Next" and "Remove" as prompted.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** SMBv1 is a legacy protocol that uses the MD5 algorithm as part of SMB. MD5 is known to be vulnerable to a number of attacks such as collision and preimage attacks and is not FIPS compliant.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have the Server Message Block (SMB) v1 protocol disabled on the SMB server.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters | SMB1 | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Configure SMBv1 Server | "Disabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters' -Name 'SMB1' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'SMB1'
```

Expected: SMB1 = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters" /v "SMB1"
```

Expected: SMB1 = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Different methods are available to disable SMBv1 on Windows Server 2022, if WN22-00-000380 is configured, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters\

Value Name: SMB1

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> Configure SMBv1 Server to "Disabled".

The system must be restarted for the change to take effect.

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and "SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

### V-254278 · WN22-00-000410 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must not have Windows PowerShell 2.0 installed.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254278r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Least Functionality: Remove Unneeded Software, PowerShell & Scripting Security |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must not have Windows PowerShell 2.0 installed.

**Why it matters:** Every program on a computer is another possible way in for an attacker. This rule removes software the system doesn't need, especially old programs known to be unsafe. It's like clearing clutter out of a house: fewer things lying around means fewer things that can be broken or misused.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-WindowsFeature | Where Name -eq PowerShell-v2
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows Server, remove roles and features with 'Uninstall-WindowsFeature <Name>' or through Server Manager. On client OSes, use 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName <Name>'. Verify with 'Get-WindowsFeature | Where Installed' or 'Get-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online'.

**Also related (PowerShell & Scripting Security):** On Windows, configure these under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Windows PowerShell: 'Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging' (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging EnableScriptBlockLogging = 1) and 'Turn on PowerShell Transcription'. Logs go to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. Write transcripts to a protected, centrally collected location.

**Operational impact:** Check that no application depends on the component before removing it (e.g. legacy scripts using PowerShell 2.0, tools that shell out to telnet or ftp). Keep a record of what was removed so it can be restored if a mission requirement is identified.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Open "PowerShell".

Enter "Get-WindowsFeature | Where Name -eq PowerShell-v2".

If "Installed State" is "Installed", this is a finding.

An Installed State of "Available" or "Removed" is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Uninstall the "Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine".

Start "Server Manager".

Select the server with the feature.

Scroll down to "ROLES AND FEATURES" in the right pane.

Select "Remove Roles and Features" from the drop-down "TASKS" list.

Select the appropriate server on the "Server Selection" page and click "Next".

Deselect "Windows PowerShell 2.0 Engine" under "Windows PowerShell" on the "Features" page.

Click "Next" and "Remove" as prompted.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Windows PowerShell 5.x added advanced logging features that can provide additional detail when malware has been run on a system. Disabling the Windows PowerShell 2.0 mitigates against a downgrade attack that evades the Windows PowerShell 5.x script block logging feature.

**Threat & control context:** Every installed package, role and feature is potential attack surface, and some (telnet, rsh, TFTP, SMBv1, PowerShell 2.0) are inherently insecure or allow security controls to be bypassed. For example, PowerShell 2.0 bypasses script-block logging and AMSI. CM-7 (least functionality) and CM-7(1)/(2) require removing what isn't mission-necessary. Removal also reduces patch burden and false positives in vulnerability scans.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services; T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter; T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell; T1059.005 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic; T1562.003 Impair Defenses: Impair Command History Logging

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-254281 · WN22-00-000440 · CAT III: The Windows Server 2022 time service must synchronize with an appropriate DoW time source.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254281r1256689_rule` |
| Severity | CAT III (low) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000355-GPOS-00143 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization, Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-004923, CCI-001891 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-45 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-8 (1) (a) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's time service must synchronize with an appropriate DoW time source.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Low priority (CAT III): This setting adds an extra layer of protection. A gap here on its own is less likely to cause harm, but it weakens the overall defenses.

**Key terms:**
- *DoD / DoW*: Department of Defense (renamed Department of War in recent DISA publications).
- *NTP / chrony*: Network Time Protocol: how computers keep their clocks accurate over the network.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service | Time Providers. Change "Configure Windows NTP Client | "Enabled", and configure the "NtpServer" field to point to an appropriate DoW time server |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-ADDomain | FT PDCEmulator
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
gpresult /scope computer /h "%TEMP%\gpresult.html" /f && start "" "%TEMP%\gpresult.html"
```

Expected: Find "Time Providers. Change "Configure Windows NTP Client" in the report: it must be "Enabled", and configure the "NtpServer" field to point to an appropriate DoW time server. Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, domain members sync from the domain hierarchy (NT5DS). The PDC emulator must point to an authoritative source using Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers >> 'Configure Windows NTP Client'. Verify with 'w32tm /query /status'.

**Also related (Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features):** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the Windows time service configuration.

Open an elevated "Command Prompt" (run as administrator).

Enter "W32tm /query /configuration".

Domain-joined systems (excluding the domain controller with the PDC emulator role):

If the value for "Type" under "NTP Client" is not "NT5DS", this is a finding.

Other systems:

If systems are configured with a "Type" of "NTP", including standalone or nondomain-joined systems and the domain controller with the PDC Emulator role, and do not have a DoW time server defined for "NTPServer", this is a finding.

To determine the domain controller with the PDC Emulator role:

Open "PowerShell".

Enter "Get-ADDomain | FT PDCEmulator".
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system to synchronize time with an appropriate DoW time source.

Domain-joined systems use NT5DS to synchronize time from other systems in the domain by default.

If the system needs to be configured to an NTP server, configure the system to point to an authorized time server by setting the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers. Change "Configure Windows NTP Client" to "Enabled", and configure the "NtpServer" field to point to an appropriate DoW time server.

The US Naval Observatory operates stratum 1 time servers, identified at https://www.cnmoc.usff.navy.mil/Our-Commands/United-States-Naval-Observatory/Precise-Time-Department/Network-Time-Protocol-NTP/. Time synchronization will occur through a hierarchy of time servers down to the local level. Clients and lower-level servers will synchronize with an authorized time server in the hierarchy.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The Windows Time Service controls time synchronization settings. Time synchronization is essential for authentication and auditing purposes. If the Windows Time Service is used, it must synchronize with a secure, authorized time source. Domain-joined systems are automatically configured to synchronize with domain controllers. If an NTP server is configured, it must synchronize with a secure, authorized time source.

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT III: any vulnerability whose existence degrades measures to protect against loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004923**: Compare the internal system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: SC-45 (1) (a) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001891**: The information system compares internal information system clocks on an organization-defined frequency with an organization-defined authoritative time source.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: AU-8 (1) (a) · Rev 3: n/a
