### V-254282 · WN22-00-000450 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must have orphaned security identifiers (SIDs) removed from user rights.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254282r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have orphaned security identifiers (SIDs) removed from user rights.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '\*S-1-5-21-'
```

Expected: Every domain/local SID listed must resolve to an existing account; unresolved SIDs are orphaned. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Review the effective User Rights setting in Local Group Policy Editor.
Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

Review each User Right listed for any unresolved SIDs to determine whether they are valid, such as due to being temporarily disconnected from the domain. (Unresolved SIDs have the format that begins with "*S-1-".)

If any unresolved SIDs exist and are not for currently valid accounts or groups, this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /export /areas USER_RIGHTS /cfg c:\path\UserRights.txt

The results in the file identify user right assignments by SID instead of group name. Review the SIDs for unidentified ones. A list of typical SIDs \ Groups is below, search Microsoft for articles on well known SIDs for others.

If any unresolved SIDs exist and are not for currently valid accounts or groups, this is a finding.

SID - Group
S-1-5-11 - Authenticated Users
S-1-5-113 - Local account
S-1-5-114 - Local account and member of Administrators group
S-1-5-19 - Local Service
S-1-5-20 - Network Service
S-1-5-32-544 - Administrators
S-1-5-32-546 - Guests
S-1-5-6 - Service
S-1-5-9 - Enterprise Domain Controllers
S-1-5-domain-512 - Domain Admins
S-1-5-root domain-519 - Enterprise Admins
S-1-5-80-3139157870-2983391045-3678747466-658725712-1809340420 - NT Service\WdiServiceHost
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove any unresolved SIDs found in User Rights assignments and determined to not be for currently valid accounts or groups by removing the accounts or groups from the appropriate group policy.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Accounts or groups given rights on a system may show up as unresolved SIDs for various reasons including deletion of the accounts or groups. If the account or group objects are reanimated, there is a potential they may still have rights no longer intended. Valid domain accounts or groups may also show up as unresolved SIDs if a connection to the domain cannot be established.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-254283 · WN22-00-000460 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 systems must have Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware and be configured to run in UEFI mode, not Legacy BIOS.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254283r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Boot Process & Console Security |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware and be configured to run in UEFI mode, not Legacy BIOS.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UEFI / Secure Boot*: Modern computer firmware and its feature that only lets trusted software start the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
$env:firmware_type
```

Expected: UEFI (not Legacy).

**How it works:** On Windows, Secure Boot and the TPM are verified with 'Confirm-SecureBootUEFI' and 'Get-Tpm'. Firmware must be UEFI, not Legacy BIOS. Boot-time protection also comes from BitLocker and the Early Launch Antimalware policy.

**Operational impact:** Store the boot-loader password in the system's credential vault, because you'll need it for kernel-parameter troubleshooting. Converting Legacy BIOS installs to UEFI generally requires MBR2GPT or a rebuild.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Devices that have UEFI firmware must run in "UEFI" mode.

Verify the system firmware is configured to run in "UEFI" mode, not "Legacy BIOS".

Run "System Information".

Under "System Summary", if "BIOS Mode" does not display "UEFI", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure UEFI firmware to run in "UEFI" mode, not "Legacy BIOS" mode.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** UEFI provides additional security features in comparison to legacy BIOS firmware, including Secure Boot. UEFI is required to support additional security features in Windows, including Virtualization Based Security and Credential Guard. Systems with UEFI that are operating in "Legacy BIOS" mode will not support these security features.

**Threat & control context:** Anyone with console or hypervisor access can interrupt the boot process to edit kernel parameters (e.g. 'init=/bin/bash'), boot into single-user or rescue mode, or load an untrusted boot loader, bypassing all OS authentication. A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1542 Pre-OS Boot; T1542.003 Pre-OS Boot: Bootkit; T1529 System Shutdown/Reboot

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must have Secure Boot enabled.

**Why it matters:** While a computer is starting up, before the normal sign-in screen appears, there are special "maintenance doors" that can skip the usual security. This rule puts locks on those doors and makes sure the computer only starts with trusted software, like making sure nobody can hot-wire a car by tampering with it before the key is turned.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *UEFI / Secure Boot*: Modern computer firmware and its feature that only lets trusted software start the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text

```

If Secure Boot is turned off, these security features will not function.

A boot-loader password, authenticated rescue modes and UEFI Secure Boot close this path (AC-3, CM-6, SI-7(9) boot process integrity). Disabling Ctrl-Alt-Del and similar console actions prevents accidental or malicious reboots (availability).

### V-254285 · WN22-AC-000010 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 account lockout duration must be configured to 15 minutes or greater.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254285r958736_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000329-GPOS-00128 |
| Topic | Account Lockout |
| CCI | CCI-002238 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-7 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's account lockout duration must be configured to 15 minutes or greater.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy | Account lockout duration | "15" minutes or greater |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^LockoutDuration\b'
```

Expected: LockoutDuration matches the required value: "15" minutes or greater. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet && findstr /i /b "LockoutDuration" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: LockoutDuration matches the required value: "15" minutes or greater. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
net accounts
```

Expected: Check the line for 'Account lockout duration': "15" minutes or greater. (Local policy view; use 'net accounts /domain' for the domain policy.)

**How it works:** Windows configures this under Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy (threshold, duration, reset counter). For domain accounts it is set in the Default Domain Policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy, and local policy affects only local accounts.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy.

If the "Account lockout duration" is less than "15" minutes (excluding "0"), this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas SecurityPolicy /CFG C:\Path\FileName.Txt

If "LockoutDuration" is less than "15" (excluding "0") in the file, this is a finding.

Configuring this to "0", requiring an administrator to unlock the account, is more restrictive and is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy >> Account lockout duration to "15" minutes or greater.

A value of "0" is also acceptable, requiring an administrator to unlock the account.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The account lockout feature, when enabled, prevents brute-force password attacks on the system. This parameter specifies the period of time that an account will remain locked after the specified number of failed logon attempts.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002238**: Automatically lock the account or node for either an organization-defined time period, until the locked account or node is released by an administrator, or delays the next logon prompt according to the organization-defined delay algorithm when the maximum number of unsuccessful logon attempts is exceeded.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 b · Rev 4: AC-7 b · Rev 3: n/a

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The account lockout feature, when enabled, prevents brute-force password attacks on the system. Secedit /Export /Areas SecurityPolicy /CFG C:\Path\FileName.Txt

```text
If "ResetLockoutCount" is less than "15" in the file, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy >> Reset account lockout counter after to at least "15" minutes.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The account lockout feature, when enabled, prevents brute-force password attacks on the system. This parameter specifies the period of time that must pass after failed logon attempts before the counter is reset to "0". The smaller this value is, the less effective the account lockout feature will be in protecting the local system.

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000044**: Enforce the organization-defined limit of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during the organization-defined time period.  
  Rev 5: AC-7 a · Rev 4: AC-7 a · Rev 3: AC-7 a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's password history must be configured to 24 passwords remembered.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Enforce password history | "24" passwords remembered |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^PasswordHistorySize\b'
```

Expected: PasswordHistorySize matches the required value: "24" passwords remembered. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet && findstr /i /b "PasswordHistorySize" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: PasswordHistorySize matches the required value: "24" passwords remembered. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
net accounts
```

Expected: Check the line for 'Enforce password history': "24" passwords remembered. (Local policy view; use 'net accounts /domain' for the domain policy.)

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for "Enforce password history" is less than "24" passwords remembered, this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas SecurityPolicy /CFG C:\Path\FileName.Txt

If "PasswordHistorySize" is less than "24" in the file, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> Enforce password history to "24" passwords remembered.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A system is more vulnerable to unauthorized access when system users recycle the same password several times without being required to change to a unique password on a regularly scheduled basis. This enables users to effectively negate the purpose of mandating periodic password changes. The default value is "24" for Windows domain systems. DoW has decided this is the appropriate value for all Windows systems.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004061**: For password-based authentication, verify when users create or update passwords, that the passwords are not found on the list of commonly-used, expected, or compromised passwords in IA-5 (1) (a).  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (b) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's minimum password length must be configured to 14 characters.

**Why it matters:** This sets the rules for how strong a password must be: long enough, and mixing capitals, lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Short or simple passwords can be guessed by computers in seconds. A long, varied password is like a key with many unique notches that's much harder to copy.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**


Expected: MinimumPasswordLength matches the required value: "14" characters. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
net accounts
```

Expected: Check the line for 'Minimum password length': "14" characters. (Local policy view; use 'net accounts /domain' for the domain policy.)

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy ('Minimum password length', 'Password must meet complexity requirements'). Domain-wide values come from the Default Domain Policy or Fine-Grained Password Policies (PSOs). Lengths above 14 require the 'Relax minimum password length limits' setting on newer builds.

**Operational impact:** Takes effect at each user's next password change. Communicate the new requirements beforehand, and check that provisioning scripts and self-service reset portals can generate compliant passwords.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for the "Minimum password length," is less than "14" characters, this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas SecurityPolicy /CFG C:\Path\FileName.Txt

If "MinimumPasswordLength" is less than "14" in the file, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> "Minimum password length" to "14" characters.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Information systems not protected with strong password schemes (including passwords of minimum length) provide the opportunity for anyone to crack the password, thus gaining access to the system and compromising the device, information, or the local network.

**Threat & control context:** Length and composition rules raise the cost of both online guessing and offline cracking of captured hashes (IA-5(1)). DoD still requires a 15-character minimum with character-class rules, while NIST SP 800-63B now favors length plus breached-password screening over composition rules. Where the two conflict, the STIG governs for DoD systems. Note that complexity rules apply only when a password is changed, so assess the age of existing passwords too.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004066**: For password-based authentication, enforce organization-defined composition and complexity rules.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (h) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000205**: The information system enforces minimum password length.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (a) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (a)

| Field | Value |

| Rule ID | `SV-254293r1051095_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000073-GPOS-00041 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-5 (1) (d) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | IA-5 (1) (c) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's reversible password encryption must be disabled.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy | Store passwords using reversible encryption | "Disabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^ClearTextPassword\b'
```

Expected: ClearTextPassword matches the required value: "Disabled". Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet && findstr /i /b "ClearTextPassword" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: ClearTextPassword matches the required value: "Disabled". Run elevated.

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy.

If the value for "Store passwords using reversible encryption" is not set to "Disabled", this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas SecurityPolicy /CFG C:\Path\FileName.Txt

If "ClearTextPassword" equals "1" in the file, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Password Policy >> Store passwords using reversible encryption to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Storing passwords using reversible encryption is essentially the same as storing clear-text versions of the passwords, which are easily compromised. For this reason, this policy must never be enabled.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-004062**: For password-based authentication, store passwords using an approved salted key derivation function, preferably using a keyed hash.  
  Rev 5: IA-5 (1) (d) · Rev 4: n/a · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-000196**: The information system, for password-based authentication, stores only cryptographically-protected passwords.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-5 (1) (c) · Rev 3: IA-5 (1) (c)

### V-254294 · WN22-AU-000010 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 audit records must be backed up to a different system or media than the system being audited.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254294r958754_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000342-GPOS-00133 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001851 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's audit records must be backed up to a different system or media than the system being audited.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Determine if a process to back up log data to a different system or media than the system being audited has been implemented.

If it has not, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Establish and implement a process for backing up log data to another system or media other than the system being audited.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protection of log data includes ensuring the log data is not accidentally lost or deleted. Audit information stored in one location is vulnerable to accidental or incidental deletion or alteration.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001851**: Transfer audit logs per organization-defined frequency to a different system, system component, or media than the system or system component conducting the logging.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 (1) · Rev 4: AU-4 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254295 · WN22-AU-000020 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must, at a minimum, offload audit records of interconnected systems in real time and offload standalone or nondomain-joined systems weekly.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254295r959008_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000479-GPOS-00224 |
| Topic | Audit Log Capacity, Offloading & Failure Handling, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-001851 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-4 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must, at a minimum, offload audit records of interconnected systems in real time and offload standalone or nondomain-joined systems weekly.

**Why it matters:** The computer keeps a "security diary" of important events. This rule makes sure the diary has enough pages, that a copy is sent to a separate, safe location, and that someone is alerted if the diary fills up or stops working. It's like a store's security cameras recording to an off-site server so a thief can't simply take the tape.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, event log sizes are set under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> Event Log Service >> Application/Security/System >> 'Specify the maximum log file size (KB)'. Forward events with Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) or a SIEM agent. Retention behavior is configured in the same policy node.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** Actions such as 'halt' or 'single' on disk-full prioritize integrity over availability and can take a production system down. Agree the action with the ISSO/AO and monitor free space proactively. Larger local logs consume disk; forwarding requires network connectivity and certificates for TLS.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the audit records, at a minimum, are offloaded for interconnected systems in real time and offloaded for standalone or nondomain-joined systems weekly.

If they are not, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the system to, at a minimum, offload audit records of interconnected systems in real time and offload standalone or nondomain-joined systems weekly.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protection of log data includes assuring the log data is not accidentally lost or deleted. Audit information stored in one location is vulnerable to accidental or incidental deletion or alteration.

**Threat & control context:** Logs that roll over, fill the disk or exist only on the compromised host can't support incident response. Attackers routinely clear or flood local logs. AU-4 (storage capacity), AU-4(1) (transfer to alternate storage), AU-5 (response to processing failures) and AU-9(2) (backup onto a separate system) require sized local storage, real-time off-host forwarding, and defined behavior (alert, halt or single-user) when audit capability is lost. Validate end-to-end delivery at the SIEM, not just the client configuration.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070 Indicator Removal; T1562.006 Impair Defenses: Indicator Blocking; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001851**: Transfer audit logs per organization-defined frequency to a different system, system component, or media than the system or system component conducting the logging.  
  Rev 5: AU-4 (1) · Rev 4: AU-4 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254296 · WN22-AU-000030 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 permissions for the Application event log must prevent access by nonprivileged accounts.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254296r958434_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000057-GPOS-00027 |
| Topic | Audit Log & Tool Protection, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-000162, CCI-000163, CCI-000164 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's permissions for the Application event log must prevent access by nonprivileged accounts.

**Why it matters:** The security diary is only useful if nobody can secretly edit or tear pages out of it. This rule locks down who can read or change the logs and the tools that manage them. It's like keeping the security camera footage in a locked room that only a couple of trusted people can enter.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
icacls %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\Application.evtx
```

Expected: Only Eventlog, SYSTEM and Administrators with Full Control.

**How it works:** On Windows, event log file permissions are on %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx. The default ACL (Eventlog service, SYSTEM, Administrators) must not be broadened. The 'Manage auditing and security log' user right must be limited to Administrators.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** With '-e 2', any later audit rule change requires a reboot to take effect, so schedule audit rule updates in maintenance windows.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Navigate to the Application event log file.

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs" folder. However, the logs may have been moved to another folder.

If the permissions for the "Application.evtx" file are not as restrictive as the default permissions listed below, this is a finding:

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the permissions on the Application event log file (Application.evtx) to prevent access by nonprivileged accounts. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement:

Eventlog - Full Control
SYSTEM - Full Control
Administrators - Full Control

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs" folder.

If the location of the logs has been changed, when adding Eventlog to the permissions, it must be entered as "NT Service\Eventlog".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. The Application event log may be susceptible to tampering if proper permissions are not applied.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000057-GPOS-00027, SRG-OS-000058-GPOS-00028, SRG-OS-000059-GPOS-00029

**Threat & control context:** If a non-privileged user, or an attacker running as one, can read, alter or delete audit data or reconfigure the audit subsystem, the audit trail loses its evidentiary value. AU-9 (protection of audit information) together with AU-9(3) (cryptographic protection) and AU-9(4) (access by subset of privileged users) require restrictive ownership and modes on logs and tools, integrity verification of audit binaries (via AIDE), and immutable audit rules ('-e 2') so the rule set can't be changed without a reboot.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.002 Indicator Removal: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs; T1070.001 Indicator Removal: Clear Windows Event Logs; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000162**: Protect audit information from unauthorized access.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-000163**: Protect audit information from unauthorized modification.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-000164**: Protect audit information from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

### V-254299 · WN22-AU-000060 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 Event Viewer must be protected from unauthorized modification and deletion.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254299r991558_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000257-GPOS-00098 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-001494, CCI-001495 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-9 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-9 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Event Viewer must be protected from unauthorized modification and deletion.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
icacls %SystemRoot%\System32\Eventvwr.exe
```

Expected: TrustedInstaller Full; Administrators, SYSTEM, Users and ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES Read & Execute only.

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This is not applicable for Windows Core Edition.

Navigate to "%SystemRoot%\System32".

View the permissions on "Eventvwr.exe".

If any groups or accounts other than TrustedInstaller have "Full control" or "Modify" permissions, this is a finding.

The default permissions below satisfy this requirement:

TrustedInstaller - Full Control
Administrators, SYSTEM, Users, ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES, ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read & Execute
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the permissions on the "Eventvwr.exe" file to prevent modification by any groups or accounts other than TrustedInstaller. The default permissions listed below satisfy this requirement:

TrustedInstaller - Full Control
Administrators, SYSTEM, Users, ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES, ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES - Read & Execute

The default location is the "%SystemRoot%\System32" folder.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Protecting audit information also includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Therefore, protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.

Operating systems providing tools to interface with audit information will leverage user permissions and roles identifying the user accessing the tools and the corresponding rights the user enjoys to make access decisions regarding the modification or deletion of audit tools.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000257-GPOS-00098, SRG-OS-000258-GPOS-00099

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001494**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized modification.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9
- **CCI-001495**: Protect audit tools from unauthorized deletion.  
  Rev 5: AU-9 a · Rev 4: AU-9 · Rev 3: AU-9

### V-254300 · WN22-AU-000070 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must be configured to audit Account Logon - Credential Validation successes.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254300r991578_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Account Logon - Credential Validation successes.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Logon | Audit Credential Validation | "Success" selected |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Credential Validation"
```

Expected: The 'Credential Validation' line must include Success ('Success and Failure' satisfies either). Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN22-SO-000050) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the "AuditPol" tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open "PowerShell" or a "Command Prompt" with elevated privileges ("Run as administrator").

Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the "AuditPol" settings with the following:

If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding.

Account Logon >> Credential Validation - Success
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Account Logon >> Audit Credential Validation with "Success" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Credential Validation records events related to validation tests on credentials for a user account logon.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c

### V-254309 · WN22-AU-000160 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must be configured to audit Logon/Logoff - Account Lockout failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254309r991552_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090 |
| Topic | Account Lockout, Security Event Auditing |
| CCI | CCI-000172, CCI-001404 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c, AC-2 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c, AC-2 (4) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c, AC-2 (4) |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Logon/Logoff - Account Lockout failures.

**Why it matters:** If someone types the wrong password a few times in a row, the account is temporarily locked so they can't keep guessing. It's like a phone that freezes after several wrong passcodes, which stops a thief from trying every possible combination.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff | Audit Account Lockout | "Failure" selected |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Account Lockout"
```

Expected: The 'Account Lockout' line must include Failure ('Success and Failure' satisfies either). Run elevated.

**How it works:** Windows configures this under Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Account Lockout Policy (threshold, duration, reset counter). For domain accounts it is set in the Default Domain Policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy, and local policy affects only local accounts.

**Also related (Security Event Auditing):** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** Service accounts with stale cached credentials (mapped drives, scheduled tasks, mobile mail clients) can trigger repeated lockouts. Identify the lockout source (Windows Event ID 4740; faillock and audit logs on Linux) before loosening the threshold.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN22-SO-000050) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the "AuditPol" tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open "PowerShell" or a "Command Prompt" with elevated privileges ("Run as administrator").

Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the "AuditPol" settings with the following:

If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding.

Logon/Logoff >> Account Lockout - Failure
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff >> Audit Account Lockout with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Account Lockout events can be used to identify potentially malicious logon attempts.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000240-GPOS-00090, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214

**Threat & control context:** Lockout thresholds turn online password guessing from an unlimited search into a handful of attempts per window (AC-7). The trade-off is denial of service: an attacker who knows usernames can deliberately lock out accounts, which is why DoD pairs a low threshold (3) with an administrator-unlock or timed-unlock requirement. Lockout does nothing against offline cracking of stolen hashes or against password spraying that stays below the threshold, so it complements, rather than replaces, password strength and MFA.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1110.001 Brute Force: Password Guessing; T1110.003 Brute Force: Password Spraying; T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
- **CCI-001404**: Automatically audit account disabling actions.  
  Rev 5: AC-2 (4) · Rev 4: AC-2 (4) · Rev 3: AC-2 (4)

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit logon successes.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff | Audit Logon | "Success" selected |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Logon"
```

Expected: The 'Logon' line must include Success ('Success and Failure' satisfies either). Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

```text

Use the "AuditPol" tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open "PowerShell" or a "Command Prompt" with elevated privileges ("Run as administrator").

Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the "AuditPol" settings with the following:

If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding.

Logon/Logoff >> Logon - Success
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Logon/Logoff >> Audit Logon with "Success" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Logon records user logons. If this is an interactive logon, it is recorded on the local system. If it is to a network share, it is recorded on the system accessed.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000032-GPOS-00013, SRG-OS-000470-GPOS-00214, SRG-OS-000472-GPOS-00217, SRG-OS-000473-GPOS-00218, SRG-OS-000475-GPOS-00220

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-254318 · WN22-AU-000250 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must be configured to audit Object Access - Removable Storage failures.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254318r991583_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000474-GPOS-00219 |
| Topic | Security Event Auditing, Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless |
| CCI | CCI-000172 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AU-12 c |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AU-12 c |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured to audit Object Access - Removable Storage failures.

**Why it matters:** This tells the computer to write down important security events in its diary, such as who logged in, who tried and failed, and who changed a setting or used admin powers. If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access | Audit Removable Storage | "Failure" selected |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Removable Storage"
```

Expected: The 'Removable Storage' line must include Failure ('Success and Failure' satisfies either). Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. Verify with 'auditpol /get /category:*'.

**Also related (Removable Media, Peripherals & Wireless):** On Windows, AutoPlay and AutoRun are under Administrative Templates >> Windows Components >> AutoPlay Policies (NoDriveTypeAutoRun = 0xFF, NoAutorun = 1). Device installation restrictions are under System >> Device Installation, and DMA protection under Kernel DMA Protection.

**Operational impact:** More audit rules mean more log volume and some CPU overhead on busy systems, particularly syscall rules on file-heavy workloads. Make sure log sizing and forwarding can handle the volume (see the audit storage rules).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Security Option "Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) to override audit policy category settings" must be set to "Enabled" (WN22-SO-000050) for the detailed auditing subcategories to be effective.

Use the "AuditPol" tool to review the current Audit Policy configuration:

Open "PowerShell" or a "Command Prompt" with elevated privileges ("Run as administrator").

Enter "AuditPol /get /category:*"

Compare the "AuditPol" settings with the following:

If the system does not audit the following, this is a finding.

Object Access >> Removable Storage - Failure

Virtual machines or systems that use network attached storage may generate excessive audit events for secondary virtual drives or the network attached storage when this setting is enabled. This may be set to Not Configured in such cases and would not be a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration >> System Audit Policies >> Object Access >> Audit Removable Storage with "Failure" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Removable Storage auditing under Object Access records events related to access attempts on file system objects on removable storage devices.

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal; T1091 Replication Through Removable Media; T1052.001 Exfiltration Over USB; T1200 Hardware Additions

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c


```text

```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Sensitive Privilege Use records events related to use of sensitive privileges, such as "Act as part of the operating system" or "Debug programs".

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000327-GPOS-00127, SRG-OS-000064-GPOS-00033, SRG-OS-000462-GPOS-00206, SRG-OS-000466-GPOS-00210

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000172**: Generate audit records for the event types defined in AU-2 c that include the audit record content defined in AU-3.  
  Rev 5: AU-12 c · Rev 4: AU-12 c · Rev 3: AU-12 c
- **CCI-002234**: Log the execution of privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (9) · Rev 4: AC-6 (9) · Rev 3: n/a

If something goes wrong, investigators can look back and see exactly what happened and who did it, much like a building's visitor sign-in log.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Audit log*: A tamper-resistant diary of security-relevant events on the computer.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
auditpol /get /subcategory:"Security State Chang"
```

Expected: The 'Security State Chang' line must include Success ('Success and Failure' satisfies either). Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Advanced Audit Policy Configuration (Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Advanced Audit Policy Configuration). Also set 'Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings' (SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy = 1), or legacy category settings may override them. System >> Security State Change - Success

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Maintaining an audit trail of system activity logs can help identify configuration errors, troubleshoot service disruptions, and analyze compromises that have occurred, as well as detect attacks. Audit logs are necessary to provide a trail of evidence in case the system or network is compromised. Collecting this data is essential for analyzing the security of information assets and detecting signs of suspicious and unexpected behavior.

Security State Change records events related to changes in the security state, such as startup and shutdown of the system.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000327-GPOS-00127, SRG-OS-000458-GPOS-00203, SRG-OS-000463-GPOS-00207, SRG-OS-000468-GPOS-00212

**Threat & control context:** Event auditing provides the detection and forensic record for nearly every other control. The STIG event set (logon/logoff, account and group management, privilege use, policy changes, use of privileged commands, permission changes, module loading, file deletion) implements AU-2 / AU-12 (event logging and generation), AU-3 (content) and AC-2(4) (automated audit of account actions). Coverage gaps translate directly into blind spots: an attacker's privilege escalation or persistence step that isn't logged can't be detected or reconstructed.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1562.002 Impair Defenses: Disable Windows Event Logging; T1562.012 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System; T1070 Indicator Removal

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.
