### V-254494 · WN22-UR-000040 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 back up files and directories user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254494r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's back up files and directories user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Back up files and directories | Only: Administrators |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^SeBackupPrivilege\b'
```

Expected: SeBackupPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet && findstr /i /b "SeBackupPrivilege" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: SeBackupPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups other than the following are granted the "Back up files and directories" user right, this is a finding:

- Administrators

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs other than the following are granted the "SeBackupPrivilege" user right, this is a finding:

S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators)

If an application requires this user right, this would not be a finding.

Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right.

The requirement must be documented with the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).

The application account must meet requirements for application account passwords, such as length (WN22-00-000050) and required frequency of changes (WN22-00-000060).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Back up files and directories to include only the following accounts or groups:

- Administrators
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Back up files and directories" user right can circumvent file and directory permissions and could allow access to sensitive data.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a


**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Create permanent shared objects to be defined but containing no entries (blank).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Create permanent shared objects" user right could expose sensitive data by creating shared objects.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |

| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | All servers (DC and member) |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's create symbolic links user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Create symbolic links | Only: Administrators |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege\b'
```

Expected: SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet && findstr /i /b "SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups other than the following are granted the "Create symbolic links" user right, this is a finding:

- Administrators

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs other than the following are granted the "SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege" user right, this is a finding:

S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Create symbolic links to include only the following accounts or groups:

- Administrators

Systems that have the Hyper-V role will also have "Virtual Machines" given this user right. If this needs to be added manually, enter it as "NT Virtual Machine\Virtual Machines".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Create symbolic links" user right can create pointers to other objects, which could expose the system to attack.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups other than the following are granted the "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right, this is a finding:

- Administrators
- Service
- Local Service
- Network Service

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs other than the following are granted the "SeImpersonatePrivilege" user right, this is a finding:

S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators)
S-1-5-6 (Service)
S-1-5-19 (Local Service)
S-1-5-20 (Network Service)

If an application requires this user right, this would not be a finding.

Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right.

The requirement must be documented with the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).

The application account must meet requirements for application account passwords, such as length (WN22-00-000050) and required frequency of changes (WN22-00-000060).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Impersonate a client after authentication to include only the following accounts or groups:

- Administrators
- Service
- Local Service
- Network Service
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Impersonate a client after authentication" user right allows a program to impersonate another user or account to run on their behalf. An attacker could use this to elevate privileges.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's modify firmware environment values user right must only be assigned to the Administrators group.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Modify firmware environment values | Only: Administrators |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege\b'
```

Expected: SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

```text

```

Expected: SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege lists only: Administrators. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups other than the following are granted the "Modify firmware environment values" user right, this is a finding:

- Administrators

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs other than the following are granted the "SeSystemEnvironmentPrivilege" user right, this is a finding:

S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Modify firmware environment values to include only the following accounts or groups:

- Administrators
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Modify firmware environment values" user right can change hardware configuration environment variables. This could result in hardware failures or a denial of service.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must only allow administrators responsible for the domain controller to have Administrator rights on the system.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'
```

Expected: Only accounts responsible for administering this system. On a domain controller use: Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'; Get-ADGroupMember 'Enterprise Admins'.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. A separate version applies to other systems.

Review the Administrators group. Only the appropriate administrator groups or accounts responsible for administration of the system may be members of the group.

Standard user accounts must not be members of the local administrator group.

If prohibited accounts are members of the local administrators group, this is a finding.

If the built-in Administrator account or other required administrative accounts are found on the system, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the Administrators group to include only administrator groups or accounts that are responsible for the system.

Remove any standard user accounts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An account that does not have Administrator duties must not have Administrator rights. Such rights would allow the account to bypass or modify required security restrictions on that machine and make it vulnerable to attack.

System administrators must log on to systems using only accounts with the minimum level of authority necessary.

Standard user accounts must not be members of the built-in Administrators group.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254386 · WN22-DC-000020 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 Kerberos user logon restrictions must be enforced.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254386r1051101_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000112-GPOS-00057 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA) |
| CCI | CCI-001941, CCI-001942 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (8) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (8), IA-2 (9) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Kerberos user logon restrictions must be enforced.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kerberos*: The ticket-based sign-in system used by Windows domains and some Linux systems.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Policies >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy | Enforce user logon restrictions | "Enabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^TicketValidateClient\b'
```

Expected: TicketValidateClient matches the required value: "Enabled". Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet && findstr /i /b "TicketValidateClient" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: TicketValidateClient matches the required value: "Enabled". Run elevated.

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Verify the following is configured in the Default Domain Policy:

Open "Group Policy Management".

Navigate to "Group Policy Objects" in the Domain being reviewed (Forest >> Domains >> Domain).

Right-click on the "Default Domain Policy".

Select "Edit".

Navigate to Computer Configuration >> Policies >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy.

If the "Enforce user logon restrictions" is not set to "Enabled", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value in the Default Domain Policy for Computer Configuration >> Policies >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy >> Enforce user logon restrictions to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This policy setting determines whether the Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) validates every request for a session ticket against the user rights policy of the target computer. The policy is enabled by default, which is the most secure setting for validating that access to target resources is not circumvented.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000112-GPOS-00057, SRG-OS-000113-GPOS-00058

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001941**: Implement replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for access to privileged accounts and/or non-privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (8) · Rev 4: IA-2 (8) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001942**: The information system implements replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to non-privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-2 (9) · Rev 3: n/a

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** In Kerberos, there are two types of tickets: Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) and Service Tickets. Upon startup, each computer gets a TGT before requesting a service ticket to the domain controller and any other computers it needs to access. For services that start up under a specified user account, users must always get a TGT first and then get Service Tickets to all computers and services accessed.

### V-254390 · WN22-DC-000060 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 computer clock synchronization tolerance must be limited to five minutes or less.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254390r1051105_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000112-GPOS-00057 |
| Topic | Time Synchronization, Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features |
| CCI | CCI-001941, CCI-001942 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-2 (8) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-2 (8), IA-2 (9) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's computer clock synchronization tolerance must be limited to five minutes or less.

**Why it matters:** This keeps the computer's clock exactly in step with an official time source. That might sound minor, but security logs from different computers can only be pieced together if every clock agrees, and some sign-in systems refuse to work when clocks drift. It's like making sure all the witnesses' watches show the same time.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *Kerberos*: The ticket-based sign-in system used by Windows domains and some Linux systems.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy | Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization | a maximum of "5" minutes or less |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^MaxClockSkew\b'
```

Expected: MaxClockSkew matches the required value: a maximum of "5" minutes or less. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas SECURITYPOLICY /quiet && findstr /i /b "MaxClockSkew" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: MaxClockSkew matches the required value: a maximum of "5" minutes or less. Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows, domain members sync from the domain hierarchy (NT5DS). The PDC emulator must point to an authoritative source using Administrative Templates >> System >> Windows Time Service >> Time Providers >> 'Configure Windows NTP Client'. Verify with 'w32tm /query /status'.

**Also related (Telemetry, Cloud & Consumer Features):** On Windows these are mostly Administrative Templates under Windows Components (Data Collection and Preview Builds, Cloud Content, Search, Store, OneDrive, Windows Error Reporting, App Privacy) and the Microsoft Edge templates. Verify the registry values under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\... as shown in each check.

**Operational impact:** Large clock corrections can confuse running applications. chrony slews gradually by default. Make sure the time servers are reachable through the firewall (UDP 123).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Verify the following is configured in the Default Domain Policy:

Open "Group Policy Management".

Navigate to "Group Policy Objects" in the Domain being reviewed (Forest >> Domains >> Domain).

Right-click on the "Default Domain Policy".

Select "Edit".

Navigate to Computer Configuration >> Policies >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy.

If the "Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization" is greater than "5" minutes, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value in the Default Domain Policy for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Account Policies >> Kerberos Policy >> Maximum tolerance for computer clock synchronization to a maximum of "5" minutes or less.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** This setting determines the maximum time difference (in minutes) that Kerberos will tolerate between the time on a client's clock and the time on a server's clock while still considering the two clocks synchronous. To prevent replay attacks, Kerberos uses timestamps as part of its protocol definition. For timestamps to work properly, the clocks of the client and the server need to be in sync as much as possible.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000112-GPOS-00057, SRG-OS-000113-GPOS-00058

**Threat & control context:** Accurate, synchronized time underpins log correlation across systems, Kerberos authentication (5-minute skew tolerance), certificate validity checks and forensic timelines (AU-8, AU-8(1) synchronization with an authoritative source, AU-8(2) secondary source). Time sources should be authenticated where possible and restricted to client mode, so the host can't be abused as an NTP amplifier.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1070.006 Indicator Removal: Timestomp; T1567 Exfiltration Over Web Service; T1213 Data from Information Repositories

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001941**: Implement replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for access to privileged accounts and/or non-privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: IA-2 (8) · Rev 4: IA-2 (8) · Rev 3: n/a
- **CCI-001942**: The information system implements replay-resistant authentication mechanisms for network access to non-privileged accounts.  
  Rev 5: n/a · Rev 4: IA-2 (9) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254391 · WN22-DC-000070 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 permissions on the Active Directory data files must only allow System and Administrators access.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254391r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions, Active Directory & Domain Controller Security |
| CCI | CCI-001314, CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-11 b, AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SI-11 b, AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SI-11 c |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's permissions on the Active Directory data files must only allow System and Administrators access.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (from DISA check text)

```text
icacls *.*
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Also related (Active Directory & Domain Controller Security):** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Run "Regedit".

Navigate to "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters".

Note the directory locations in the values for:

Database log files path
DSA Database file

By default, they will be \Windows\NTDS.

If the locations are different, the following will need to be run for each.

Open "Command Prompt (Admin)".

Navigate to the NTDS directory (\Windows\NTDS by default).

Run "icacls *.*".

If the permissions on each file are not as restrictive as the following, this is a finding:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)

(I) - permission inherited from parent container
(F) - full access
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the permissions on NTDS database and log files as follows:

NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(I)(F)
BUILTIN\Administrators:(I)(F)

(I) - permission inherited from parent container
(F) - full access
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Improper access permissions for directory data-related files could allow unauthorized users to read, modify, or delete directory data or audit trails.

Satisfies: SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125, SRG-OS-000206-GPOS-00084

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001314**: Reveal error messages only to organization-defined personnel or roles.  
  Rev 5: SI-11 b · Rev 4: SI-11 b · Rev 3: SI-11 c
- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254392 · WN22-DC-000080 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 Active Directory SYSVOL directory must have the proper access control permissions.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254392r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Active Directory SYSVOL directory must have the proper access control permissions.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (from DISA check text)

```text
net share
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*CMD* (from DISA check text)

```text
icacls c:\Windows\SYSVOL
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*CMD* (from DISA check text)

```text
icacls /help
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Open a command prompt.

Run "net share".

Make note of the directory location of the SYSVOL share.

By default, this will be \Windows\SYSVOL\sysvol. For this requirement, permissions will be verified at the first SYSVOL directory level.

If any standard user accounts or groups have greater than "Read & execute" permissions, this is a finding.

The default permissions noted below meet this requirement:

Open "Command Prompt".

Run "icacls c:\Windows\SYSVOL".

The following results must be displayed:

NT AUTHORITY\Authenticated Users:(RX)
NT AUTHORITY\Authenticated Users:(OI)(CI)(IO)(GR,GE)
BUILTIN\Server Operators:(RX)
BUILTIN\Server Operators:(OI)(CI)(IO)(GR,GE)
BUILTIN\Administrators:(M,WDAC,WO)
BUILTIN\Administrators:(OI)(CI)(IO)(F)
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(F)
NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(IO)(F)
CREATOR OWNER:(OI)(CI)(IO)(F)

(RX) - Read & execute

Run "icacls /help" to view definitions of other permission codes.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the permissions on the SYSVOL directory. Do not allow greater than "Read & execute" permissions for standard user accounts or groups. The defaults below meet this requirement:

C:\Windows\SYSVOL
Type - "Allow" for all
Inherited from - "None" for all

Principal - Access - Applies to

Authenticated Users - Read & execute - This folder, subfolder, and files
Server Operators - Read & execute- This folder, subfolder, and files
Administrators - Special - This folder only (Special = Basic Permissions: all selected except Full control)
CREATOR OWNER - Full control - Subfolders and files only
Administrators - Full control - Subfolders and files only
SYSTEM - Full control - This folder, subfolders, and files
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Improper access permissions for directory data files could allow unauthorized users to read, modify, or delete directory data.

The SYSVOL directory contains public files (to the domain) such as policies and logon scripts. Data in shared subdirectories are replicated to all domain controllers in a domain.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254393 · WN22-DC-000090 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 Active Directory Group Policy objects must have proper access control permissions.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254393r1081073_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Active Directory Group Policy objects must have proper access control permissions.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Group Policy*: The central way Windows administrators push settings to many computers at once.
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Import-Module GroupPolicy; Get-GPO -All | ForEach-Object { $_.DisplayName; Get-GPPermission -Guid $_.Id -All | Format-Table Trustee, Permission -AutoSize }
```

Expected: Only authorized groups have Edit or Edit/Delete/Modify Security permissions.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Review the permissions on Group Policy objects.

Open "Group Policy Management" (available from various menus or run "gpmc.msc").

Navigate to "Group Policy Objects" in the domain being reviewed (Forest >> Domains >> Domain).

For each Group Policy object:

Select the Group Policy object item in the left pane.

Select the "Delegation" tab in the right pane.

Select "Advanced".

Select each Group or user name.

View the permissions.

If any standard user accounts or groups have "Allow" permissions greater than "Read" and "Apply group policy", this is a finding.

Other access permissions that allow the objects to be updated are considered findings unless specifically documented by the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).

The default permissions noted below satisfy this requirement.

The permissions shown are at the summary level. More detailed permissions can be viewed by selecting the next "Advanced" button, the desired Permission entry, and the "Edit" button.

Authenticated Users - Read, Apply group policy, Special permissions

The special permissions for Authenticated Users are for Read-type Properties. If detailed permissions include any Create, Delete, Modify, or Write Permissions or Properties, this is a finding.

The special permissions for the following default groups are not the focus of this requirement and may include a wide range of permissions and properties:

CREATOR OWNER - Special permissions
SYSTEM - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
Domain Admins - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
Enterprise Admins - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS - Read, Special permissions
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the permissions on Group Policy objects to not allow greater than "Read" and "Apply group policy" for standard user accounts or groups. The default permissions below meet this requirement:

Authenticated Users - Read, Apply group policy, Special permissions

The special permissions for Authenticated Users are for Read-type Properties.

CREATOR OWNER - Special permissions
SYSTEM - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
Domain Admins - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
Enterprise Admins - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Delete all child objects, Special permissions
ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS - Read, Special permissions

Document any other access permissions that allow the objects to be updated with the ISSO.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When directory service database objects do not have appropriate access control permissions, it may be possible for malicious users to create, read, update, or delete the objects and degrade or destroy the integrity of the data. When the directory service is used for identification, authentication, or authorization functions, a compromise of the database objects could lead to a compromise of all systems relying on the directory service.

For Active Directory (AD), the Group Policy objects require special attention. In a distributed administration model (i.e., help desk), Group Policy objects are more likely to have access permissions changed from the secure defaults. If inappropriate access permissions are defined for Group Policy objects, this could allow an intruder to change the security policy applied to all domain client computers (workstations and servers).

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-254395 · WN22-DC-000110 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 organization created Active Directory Organizational Unit (OU) objects must have proper access control permissions.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254395r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Active Directory & Domain Controller Security, File & Directory Permissions |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Procedural / documentation |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's organization created Active Directory Organizational Unit (OU) objects must have proper access control permissions.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Import-Module ActiveDirectory; $dn = (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName; Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter * | ForEach-Object { $_.DistinguishedName; (Get-Acl -Path "AD:$($_.DistinguishedName)").Access | Where-Object { -not $_.IsInherited } | Format-Table IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights, AccessControlType -AutoSize }
```

Expected: No unexpected identities with write, create or delete rights.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Also related (File & Directory Permissions):** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Review the permissions on domain-defined OUs.

Open "Active Directory Users and Computers" (available from various menus or run "dsa.msc").

Ensure "Advanced Features" is selected in the "View" menu.

For each OU that is defined (folder in folder icon) excluding the Domain Controllers OU:

Right-click the OU and select "Properties".

Select the "Security" tab.

If the Allow type permissions on the OU are not at least as restrictive as those below, this is a finding.

The permissions shown are at the summary level. More detailed permissions can be viewed by selecting the "Advanced" button, the desired Permission entry, and the "Edit" or "View" button.

Except where noted otherwise, the special permissions may include a wide range of permissions and properties and are acceptable for this requirement.

CREATOR OWNER - Special permissions

Self - Special permissions

Authenticated Users - Read, Special permissions

The Special permissions for Authenticated Users are Read type. If detailed permissions include any Create, Delete, Modify, or Write Permissions or Properties, this is a finding.

SYSTEM - Full Control

Domain Admins - Full Control

Enterprise Admins - Full Control

Key Admins - Special permissions

Enterprise Key Admins - Special permissions

Administrators - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Generate resultant set of policy (logging), Generate resultant set of policy (planning), Special permissions

Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access - Special permissions

The Special permissions for Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access are for Read types. If detailed permissions include any Create, Delete, Modify, or Write Permissions or Properties, this is a finding.

ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS - Read, Special permissions

If an Information System Security Officer (ISSO)-approved distributed administration model (help desk or other user support staff) is implemented, permissions above Read may be allowed for groups documented by the ISSO.

If any OU with improper permissions includes identification or authentication data (e.g., accounts, passwords, or password hash data) used by systems to determine access control, the severity is CAT I (e.g., OUs that include user accounts, including service/application accounts).

If an OU with improper permissions does not include identification and authentication data used by systems to determine access control, the severity is CAT II (e.g., Workstation, Printer OUs).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Maintain the Allow type permissions on domain-defined OUs to be at least as restrictive as the defaults below.

Document any additional permissions above Read with the ISSO if an approved distributed administration model (help desk or other user support staff) is implemented.

CREATOR OWNER - Special permissions

Self - Special permissions

Authenticated Users - Read, Special permissions

The special permissions for Authenticated Users are Read type.

SYSTEM - Full Control

Domain Admins - Full Control

Enterprise Admins - Full Control

Key Admins - Special permissions

Enterprise Key Admins - Special permissions

Administrators - Read, Write, Create all child objects, Generate resultant set of policy (logging), Generate resultant set of policy (planning), Special permissions

Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access - Special permissions

The special permissions for Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access are for Read types.

ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS - Read, Special permissions
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When directory service database objects do not have appropriate access control permissions, it may be possible for malicious users to create, read, update, or delete the objects and degrade or destroy the integrity of the data. When the directory service is used for identification, authentication, or authorization functions, a compromise of the database objects could lead to a compromise of all systems that rely on the directory service.

For Active Directory, the OU objects require special attention. In a distributed administration model (i.e., help desk), OU objects are more likely to have access permissions changed from the secure defaults. If inappropriate access permissions are defined for OU objects, it could allow an intruder to add or delete users in the OU. This could result in unauthorized access to data or a denial of service (DoS) to authorized users.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle; T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254396 · WN22-DC-000120 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 data files owned by users must be on a different logical partition from the directory server data files.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254396r1137695_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000138-GPOS-00069 |
| Topic | File & Directory Permissions, File System Layout & Mount Options |
| CCI | CCI-001090 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-4 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-4 |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's data files owned by users must be on a different logical partition from the directory server data files.

**Why it matters:** Every file on a computer has a label saying who owns it and who can read or change it. This rule makes sure sensitive files, such as the list of password fingerprints or system settings, can only be touched by the right people. It's like keeping personnel files in a locked HR cabinet rather than on the break-room table.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (from DISA check text)

```text
net share
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, check NTFS ACLs with 'icacls <path>' or 'Get-Acl'. The STIG specifies baseline ACLs for system folders, registry hives and event logs. Don't broaden the default ACLs on %SystemRoot%, Program Files or HKLM\SECURITY.

**Also related (File System Layout & Mount Options):** On Windows, NTFS is required for all local volumes. Separate data volumes are an availability practice.

**Operational impact:** Tightening permissions can break applications that read their configuration as a non-root user. Prefer group-based access over loosening the mode, and re-check after package updates, which can reset modes.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Run "Regedit".

Navigate to "HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters".

Note the directory locations in the values for "DSA Database file".

Open "Command Prompt".

Enter "net share".

Note the logical drive(s) or file system partition for any organization-created data shares.

Ignore system shares (e.g., NETLOGON, SYSVOL, and administrative shares ending in $). User shares that are hidden (ending with $) must not be ignored.

If user shares are located on the same logical partition as the directory server data files, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Move shares used to store files owned by users to a different logical partition than the directory server data files.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** When directory service data files, especially for directories used for identification, authentication, or authorization, reside on the same logical partition as user-owned files, the directory service data may be more vulnerable to unauthorized access or other availability compromises. Directory service and user-owned data files sharing a partition may be configured with less restrictive permissions in order to allow access to the user data.

The directory service may be vulnerable to a denial of service attack when user-owned files on a common partition are expanded to an extent preventing the directory service from acquiring more space for directory or audit data.

**Threat & control context:** Permissive ownership or modes on credentials (shadow, SSH host keys), libraries, system binaries, cron and boot configuration, and log files allow tampering, credential theft and execution-flow hijacking. This is AC-3 / AC-6 least privilege applied at the file-system layer, plus CM-5(6) (privilege to change software libraries). Unowned files and world-writable directories without the sticky bit are common persistence and escalation footholds.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1222 File and Directory Permissions Modification; T1574 Hijack Execution Flow; T1548.001 Abuse Elevation Control: Setuid and Setgid; T1068 Exploitation for Privilege Escalation; T1499 Endpoint Denial of Service

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001090**: Prevent unauthorized and unintended information transfer via shared system resources.  
  Rev 5: SC-4 · Rev 4: SC-4 · Rev 3: SC-4

#### Level 3: General Audience

This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing LDAP signing or channel binding breaks clients and appliances that use simple binds over unsigned LDAP. Check Directory Service event 2889 to find them before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers, it is NA for other systems.

Review the installed roles the domain controller is supporting.

Start "Server Manager".

Select "AD DS" in the left pane and the server name under "Servers" to the right.

Select "Add (or Remove) Roles and Features" from "Tasks" in the "Roles and Features" section. (Cancel before any changes are made.)

Determine if any additional server roles are installed. A basic domain controller setup will include the following:

- Active Directory Domain Services
- DNS Server
- File and Storage Services

If any roles not requiring installation on a domain controller are installed, this is a finding.

A Domain Name System (DNS) server integrated with the directory server (e.g., AD-integrated DNS) is an acceptable application. However, the DNS server must comply with the DNS STIG security requirements.

Run "Programs and Features".

Review installed applications.

If any applications are installed that are not required for the domain controller, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Remove additional roles or applications such as web, database, and email from the domain controller.
```

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Executing application servers on the same host machine with a directory server may substantially weaken the security of the directory server. Web or database server applications usually require the addition of many programs and accounts, increasing the attack surface of the computer.

Some applications require the addition of privileged accounts, providing potential sources of compromise. Some applications (such as Microsoft Exchange) may require the use of network ports or services conflicting with the directory server. In this case, nonstandard ports might be selected, and this could interfere with intrusion detection or prevention services.

**Threat & control context:** Domain controllers hold the keys to every domain identity, so DC compromise is total enterprise compromise. Requirements cover LDAP signing and channel binding (anti-relay), secure-channel signing and sealing, machine-account password rotation, protection of NTDS/SYSVOL/GPO permissions, restricting who can administer and log on to DCs, and directory auditing. These implement AC-3, AC-6, SC-8, SC-23 and AU-2 for the identity tier. Assess them alongside the administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.

**Why it matters:** In an organization, a few central servers (domain controllers) keep the master list of every user, password and permission. This rule adds extra protection to those servers and the conversations other computers have with them. It's like guarding the room that holds the master key cabinet more tightly than any other room in the building.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Procedural / documentation. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

No single command can validate this rule. It is a procedural or manual check; follow the DISA check procedure.

**How it works:** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. It is NA for other systems.

Review the organization network diagram(s) or documentation to determine the level of classification for the network(s) over which replication data is transmitted.

Determine the classification level of the Windows domain controller.

If the classification level of the Windows domain controller is higher than the level of the networks, review the organization network diagram(s) and directory implementation documentation to determine if NSA-approved encryption is used to protect the replication network traffic.

If the classification level of the Windows domain controller is higher than the level of the network traversed and NSA-approved encryption is not used, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure NSA-approved (Type 1) cryptography to protect the directory data in transit for directory service implementations at a classified confidentiality level that transfer replication data through a network cleared to a lower level than the data.
```
