Expected: SeDenyServiceLogonRight lists only: include no entries (blank). Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet && findstr /i /b "SeDenyServiceLogonRight" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: SeDenyServiceLogonRight lists only: include no entries (blank). Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Active Directory & Domain Controller Security):** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. A separate version applies to other systems.

Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups are defined for the "Deny log on as a service" user right, this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs are granted the "SeDenyServiceLogonRight" user right, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Deny log on as a service to include no entries (blank).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Deny log on as a service" user right defines accounts that are denied logon as a service.

Incorrect configurations could prevent services from starting and result in a denial of service.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-271427 · WN22-DC-000406 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must be configured for name-based strong mappings for certificates.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-271427r1137691_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be configured for name-based strong mappings for certificates.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PKI / certificates*: Public Key Infrastructure: the system of digital ID certificates and trusted issuers.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Template >> System >> KDC | Allow name-based strong mappings for certificates | "Enabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
gpresult /scope computer /h "%TEMP%\gpresult.html" /f && start "" "%TEMP%\gpresult.html"
```

Expected: Find "Allow name-based strong mappings for certificates" in the report: it must be "Enabled". Run elevated.

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to domain controllers. This is not applicable for member servers.

Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Administrative Template >> System >> KDC >> Allow name-based strong mappings for certificates.

If "Allow name-based strong mappings for certificates" is not "Enabled", this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Template >> System >> KDC >> Allow name-based strong mappings for certificates to "Enabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Weak mappings give rise to security vulnerabilities and demand hardening measures. Certificate names must be correctly mapped to the intended user account in Active Directory. A lack of strong name-based mappings allows certain weak certificate mappings, such as Issuer/Subject AltSecID and User Principal Names (UPN) mappings, to be treated as strong mappings.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-254427 · WN22-DC-000430 · CAT II: The password for the krbtgt account on a domain must be reset at least every 180 days.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254427r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Password Age, History & Reuse, Active Directory & Domain Controller Security |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | Domain controller only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** The password for the krbtgt account on a domain must be reset at least every 180 days.

**Why it matters:** This makes people change passwords every so often and stops them from simply switching back to a password they used recently. If a password was quietly stolen, it eventually stops working, a bit like changing the locks periodically in case someone copied a key.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *PowerShell*: A powerful Windows command-line and scripting tool.
- *Active Directory*: Microsoft's central directory of users, computers and permissions for an organization.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-ADUser krbtgt -Property PasswordLastSet
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

**How it works:** Windows sets this in Account Policies >> Password Policy: 'Maximum password age', 'Minimum password age', 'Enforce password history'. Domain values come from the Default Domain Policy or PSOs.

**Also related (Active Directory & Domain Controller Security):** On Windows, the relevant Security Options include 'Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements' (Require signing), 'Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)' and 'Domain member: Maximum machine account password age' (30 days). DC-specific checks review permissions on NTDS (%SystemRoot%\NTDS), SYSVOL and GPOs, and AD object auditing (SACLs). Use 'dcdiag', 'repadmin /showrepl' and ADSI Edit or 'Get-Acl AD:' to verify.

**Operational impact:** Changing login.defs does not retroactively update existing accounts, so remember to run chage for current users. Exclude non-interactive service accounts from expiry only through a documented exception (or use gMSAs on Windows).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This requirement is applicable to domain controllers; it is NA for other systems.

Open "Windows PowerShell".

Enter "Get-ADUser krbtgt -Property PasswordLastSet".

If the "PasswordLastSet" date is more than 180 days old, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Reset the password for the krbtgt account a least every 180 days. The password must be changed twice to effectively remove the password history. Changing once, waiting for replication to complete and changing again reduces the risk of issues. Changing twice in rapid succession forces clients to re-authenticate (including application services) but is desired if a compromise is suspected.

PowerShell scripts are available to accomplish this such as at the following link:

https://gallery.technet.microsoft.com/Reset-the-krbtgt-account-581a9e51

Open "Active Directory Users and Computers" (available from various menus or run "dsa.msc").

Select "Advanced Features" in the "View" menu if not previously selected.

Select the "Users" node.

Right-click on the krbtgt account and select "Reset password".

Enter a password that meets password complexity requirements.

Clear the "User must change password at next logon" check box.

The system will automatically change this to a system-generated complex password.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The krbtgt account acts as a service account for the Kerberos Key Distribution Center (KDC) service. The account and password are created when a domain is created and the password is typically not changed. If the krbtgt account is compromised, attackers can create valid Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGT).

The password must be changed twice to effectively remove the password history. Changing once, waiting for replication to complete and the amount of time equal to or greater than the maximum Kerberos ticket lifetime, and changing again reduces the risk of issues.

**Threat & control context:** Maximum age bounds the useful lifetime of a compromised credential. Minimum age plus history prevent users from cycling straight back to a known password, which would defeat the history check (IA-5(1)(d)/(e)). The trend in current guidance is to prefer event-driven rotation (on suspected compromise) over periodic rotation, but the DoD baseline values remain enforceable requirements.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

## Member server-only rules

*Apply these in addition to the common rules on member and standalone servers (STIG IDs with -MS-).*

### V-254428 · WN22-MS-000010 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 must only allow administrators responsible for the member server or standalone or nondomain-joined system to have Administrator rights on the system.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254428r958726_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Manual configuration |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must only allow administrators responsible for the member server or standalone or nondomain-joined system to have Administrator rights on the system.

**Why it matters:** Every computer comes with a few built-in "master" accounts whose names everyone knows. This rule makes those accounts harder to abuse, for example by not letting anyone log in directly as the master account and never allowing accounts with no password. It's like not leaving the master key labelled "MASTER KEY" hanging by the front door.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:** No single machine-readable setting. This is implemented via: Manual configuration. See the fix text.

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (STIG Explorer command)

```text
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'
```

Expected: Only accounts responsible for administering this system. On a domain controller use: Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'; Get-ADGroupMember 'Enterprise Admins'.

**How it works:** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Operational impact:** Make sure at least one named administrator account with sudo or admin rights works before disabling root or Administrator logon paths. Renaming the built-in Administrator can break scripts that reference it by name.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems. A separate version applies to domain controllers.

Open "Computer Management".

Navigate to "Groups" under "Local Users and Groups".

Review the local "Administrators" group.

Only administrator groups or accounts responsible for administration of the system may be members of the group.

For domain-joined member servers, the Domain Admins group must be replaced by a domain member server administrator group.

Standard user accounts must not be members of the local Administrator group.

If accounts that do not have responsibility for administration of the system are members of the local Administrators group, this is a finding.

If the built-in Administrator account or other required administrative accounts are found on the system, this is not a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the local "Administrators" group to include only administrator groups or accounts responsible for administration of the system.

For domain-joined member servers, replace the Domain Admins group with a domain member server administrator group.

Remove any standard user accounts.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** An account that does not have Administrator duties must not have Administrator rights. Such rights would allow the account to bypass or modify required security restrictions on that machine and make it vulnerable to attack.

System administrators must log on to systems using only accounts with the minimum level of authority necessary.

For domain-joined member servers, the Domain Admins group must be replaced by a domain member server administrator group (see V-243468 in the Active Directory Domain STIG). Restricting highly privileged accounts from the local Administrators group helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation resulting from credential theft attacks.

Standard user accounts must not be members of the built-in Administrators group.

**Threat & control context:** Well-known accounts (root, Administrator, Guest) are guaranteed to exist with predictable names, which makes them ideal targets. Blocking direct logon forces attribution through named accounts (IA-2, AC-6(2)). Removing empty-password acceptance eliminates trivial access, and unique local admin passwords (LAPS) break pass-the-hash lateral movement across a fleet. Assess the effective result across every access path: console, SSH, RDP and network logon.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts; T1110 Brute Force

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254429 · WN22-MS-000020 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 local administrator accounts must have their privileged token filtered to prevent elevated privileges from being used over the network on domain-joined member servers.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254429r958518_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000134-GPOS-00068 |
| Topic | Smart Card / PKI & Multifactor Authentication, Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening |
| CCI | CCI-001084 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | SC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | SC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's local administrator accounts must have their privileged token filtered to prevent elevated privileges from being used over the network on domain-joined member servers.

**Why it matters:** Instead of (or in addition to) a password, you prove who you are with something you physically carry, such as a government ID card (CAC) with a chip in it, plus a PIN. Someone who learns your PIN still can't get in without the card. It's like a bank requiring both your debit card and your PIN at the ATM.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

**Key terms:**
- *STIG*: Security Technical Implementation Guide: DoD's official checklist of security settings for a product.
- *UAC*: User Account Control: the Windows pop-up that asks for confirmation before something makes system-wide changes.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System | LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide | Apply UAC restrictions to local accounts on network logons | "Enabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System' -Name 'LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy'
```

Expected: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System" /v "LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy"
```

Expected: LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** On Windows the relevant settings are the Trusted Root / Intermediate certificate stores (deployed with the DoD InstallRoot tool or GPO) and 'Untrusted Certificates' for the cross-certificates DISA requires removing. Smart card enforcement is set per account or through 'Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card'. Verify with certlm.msc or 'Get-ChildItem Cert:\LocalMachine\Root'.

**Also related (Built-in & Privileged Account Hardening):** On Windows these are Security Options ('Accounts: Rename administrator account', 'Accounts: Guest account status', 'Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only') plus LAPS for unique, rotated local administrator passwords.

**Operational impact:** Mis-mapped certificates or stale CA bundles lock users out. Stage CA updates before old certificates expire, test revocation checking (OCSP/CRL reachability) on isolated networks, and keep a documented break-glass account.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers. For domain controllers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive:  HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path:  \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System

Value Name:  LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy

Type:  REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)

This setting may cause issues with some network scanning tools if local administrative accounts are used remotely. Scans must use domain accounts where possible. If a local administrative account must be used, temporarily enabling the privileged token by configuring the registry value to "1" may be required.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> MS Security Guide >> Apply UAC restrictions to local accounts on network logons to "Enabled".

This policy setting requires the installation of the SecGuide custom templates included with the STIG package. "SecGuide.admx" and " SecGuide.adml" must be copied to the \Windows\PolicyDefinitions and \Windows\PolicyDefinitions\en-US directories respectively.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** A compromised local administrator account can provide means for an attacker to move laterally between domain systems.

With User Account Control enabled, filtering the privileged token for local administrator accounts will prevent the elevated privileges of these accounts from being used over the network.

**Threat & control context:** Certificate-based multifactor authentication removes reusable shared secrets from the authentication path, which neutralizes password spraying, credential stuffing and most phishing. The trust store controls which CAs can issue identities the system accepts, so installing only DoD-approved roots (and removing untrusted or cross-certified ones) is an integrity control on authentication itself. Relevant controls: IA-2(1)/(2)/(12), IA-5(2) (PKI-based authentication: path validation and revocation checking), SC-17.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1078 Valid Accounts; T1110 Brute Force; T1556 Modify Authentication Process; T1078.001 Valid Accounts: Default Accounts; T1078.003 Valid Accounts: Local Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001084**: Isolate security functions from nonsecurity functions.  
  Rev 5: SC-3 · Rev 4: SC-3 · Rev 3: SC-3

### V-254430 · WN22-MS-000030 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 local users on domain-joined member servers must not be enumerated.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254430r958478_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000095-GPOS-00049 |
| Topic | Logon Screen & Desktop Settings |
| CCI | CCI-000381 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-7 a |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-7 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's local users on domain-joined member servers must not be enumerated.

**Why it matters:** This decides what the sign-in screen shows and which shortcuts are allowed. For example, it hides the list of usernames, doesn't show who signed in last, and turns off "sign in automatically". It's like a hotel front desk that won't tell a stranger which room a guest is in.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System | EnumerateLocalUsers | REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon | Enumerate local users on domain-joined computers | "Disabled" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System' -Name 'EnumerateLocalUsers' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'EnumerateLocalUsers'
```

Expected: EnumerateLocalUsers = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System" /v "EnumerateLocalUsers"
```

Expected: EnumerateLocalUsers = REG_DWORD = 0x00000000 (0). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** On Windows, use Security Options such as 'Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in' and 'Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL' (Disabled). Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon covers enumerating local users, convenience PIN and picture password. Credential User Interface >> 'Do not display the password reveal button' handles the reveal button.

**Operational impact:** Users will need to type their username in full and can't use convenience sign-in methods. Hiding restart buttons on the logon screen means console users need credentials to reboot.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers. For domain controllers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\System\

Value Name: EnumerateLocalUsers

Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000000 (0)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Logon >> Enumerate local users on domain-joined computers to "Disabled".
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The username is one part of logon credentials that could be used to gain access to a system. Preventing the enumeration of users limits this information to authorized personnel.

**Threat & control context:** The logon surface can leak information (usernames, the last logged-on user, local administrator lists) that cuts an attacker's effort in half, and convenience features (automatic logon, picture passwords, convenience PINs, password reveal buttons) weaken authentication assurance. These settings reduce information disclosure (AC-14, IA-6 authenticator feedback) and keep interactive logon on approved authenticators.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1087 Account Discovery; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000381**: Configure the system to provide only organization-defined mission essential capabilities.  
  Rev 5: CM-7 a · Rev 4: CM-7 a · Rev 3: CM-7

### V-254431 · WN22-MS-000040 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must restrict unauthenticated Remote Procedure Call (RPC) clients from connecting to the RPC server on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254431r971545_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000379-GPOS-00164 |
| Topic | File Sharing (SMB) & Anonymous Access |
| CCI | CCI-001967 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | IA-3 (1) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict unauthenticated Remote Procedure Call (RPC) clients from connecting to the RPC server on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

**Why it matters:** Computers on a network share files with each other using a system called SMB. This rule makes every file-sharing conversation carry a tamper-proof "seal" and stops strangers who haven't signed in from browsing the list of users and shared folders. It's like requiring visitors to sign in at the front desk before they can read the staff directory.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc | RestrictRemoteClients | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Procedure Call | Restrict Unauthenticated RPC clients | "Enabled" with "Authenticated" selected |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc' -Name 'RestrictRemoteClients' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'RestrictRemoteClients'
```

Expected: RestrictRemoteClients = REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc" /v "RestrictRemoteClients"
```

Expected: RestrictRemoteClients = REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** Mostly Security Options: 'Microsoft network client/server: Digitally sign communications (always)' (RequireSecuritySignature), 'Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares' (RestrictAnonymous), 'Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users', 'Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares', 'Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM'. SMBv1 is removed with 'Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol'. Check with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration'.

**Operational impact:** Mandatory signing adds CPU overhead on high-throughput file servers (usually negligible on modern hardware) and can break very old clients and some NAS devices. Restricting anonymous access can affect legacy apps that rely on null sessions.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems, it is NA for domain controllers.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive:  HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path:  \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Rpc\

Value Name:  RestrictRemoteClients

Type:  REG_DWORD
Value:  0x00000001 (1)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Remote Procedure Call >> Restrict Unauthenticated RPC clients to "Enabled" with "Authenticated" selected.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Unauthenticated RPC clients may allow anonymous access to sensitive information. Configuring RPC to restrict unauthenticated RPC clients from connecting to the RPC server will prevent anonymous connections.

**Threat & control context:** SMB is the backbone of Windows file and administrative traffic and a principal lateral-movement channel. Unsigned SMB enables NTLM relay attacks. Anonymous (null session) access and SAM/share enumeration give unauthenticated attackers reconnaissance data such as user lists and group memberships. SMBv1 lacks modern protections and was the propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya. These settings support AC-3, AC-14 (actions without identification), SC-8 and CM-7.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1135 Network Share Discovery; T1087 Account Discovery; T1021.002 Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-001967**: Authenticate organization-defined devices and/or types of devices before establishing a local, remote, and/or network connection using bidirectional authentication that is cryptographically based.  
  Rev 5: IA-3 (1) · Rev 4: IA-3 (1) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254432 · WN22-MS-000050 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must limit the caching of logon credentials to four or less on domain-joined member servers.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254432r991589_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Credential Storage & Password Hashing |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must limit the caching of logon credentials to four or less on domain-joined member servers.

**Why it matters:** Computers shouldn't store your actual password. Instead they store a scrambled "fingerprint" of it that can't be turned back into the password. This rule makes sure that fingerprint is created with a strong method, so that even if someone steals the file, they can't easily work out everyone's passwords.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon | CachedLogonsCount | REG_SZ = 4 (or less) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Interactive Logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case Domain Controller is not available) | "4" logons or less |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon' -Name 'CachedLogonsCount' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'CachedLogonsCount'
```

Expected: CachedLogonsCount = REG_SZ = 4 (or less). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" /v "CachedLogonsCount"
```

Expected: CachedLogonsCount = REG_SZ = 4 (or less). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** Relevant Windows settings include 'Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' (NoLMHash), 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' (Disabled), and 'Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache' (CachedLogonsCount).

**Operational impact:** Reducing cached logons can prevent laptop users from signing in when they are off the network. Disabling LM hashes affects only very old clients (pre-Windows 2000 era).

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers. For domain controllers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems, this is NA.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive:  HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path:  \SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\

Value Name:  CachedLogonsCount

Value Type:  REG_SZ
Value:  4 (or less)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> Interactive Logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case Domain Controller is not available) to "4" logons or less.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The default Windows configuration caches the last logon credentials for users who log on interactively to a system. This feature is provided for system availability reasons, such as the user's machine being disconnected from the network or domain controllers being unavailable. Even though the credential cache is well protected, if a system is attacked, an unauthorized individual may isolate the password to a domain user account using a password-cracking program and gain access to the domain.

**Threat & control context:** When a host is compromised, stored credential material is the attacker's path to lateral movement. Weak or reversible storage (LM hashes, reversible encryption, low-iteration hashes, excessive cached domain logons) turns a single compromise into credential recovery for many accounts. IA-5(1)(c) requires that only cryptographically protected passwords be stored and transmitted. Strong salted, iterated hashing such as SHA-512 crypt with sufficient rounds increases offline cracking cost.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1110.002 Brute Force: Password Cracking; T1552 Unsecured Credentials

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b

### V-254433 · WN22-MS-000060 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 must restrict remote calls to the Security Account Manager (SAM) to Administrators on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254433r1106522_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000324-GPOS-00125 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA) |
| CCI | CCI-002235 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-6 (10) |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | n/a |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must restrict remote calls to the Security Account Manager (SAM) to Administrators on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa | RestrictRemoteSAM | REG_SZ = O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options | Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM |  |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa' -Name 'RestrictRemoteSAM' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'RestrictRemoteSAM'
```

Expected: RestrictRemoteSAM = REG_SZ = O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v "RestrictRemoteSAM"
```

Expected: RestrictRemoteSAM = REG_SZ = O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems; it is NA for domain controllers.

If the following registry value does not exist or is not configured as specified, this is a finding:

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\

Value Name: RestrictRemoteSAM

Value Type: REG_SZ
Value: O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA)
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Navigate to the policy Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> Security Options >> Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM.

Select "Edit Security" to configure the "Security descriptor:".

Add "Administrators" in "Group or user names:" if it is not already listed (this is the default).

Select "Administrators" in "Group or user names:".

Select "Allow" for "Remote Access" in "Permissions for "Administrators".

Click "OK".

The "Security descriptor:" must be populated with "O:BAG:BAD:(A;;RC;;;BA) for the policy to be enforced.

If an application requires this user right, this would not be a finding. Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right. The requirement must be documented and approved by the information system security officer (ISSO).
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** The Windows SAM stores users' passwords. Restricting Remote Procedure Call (RPC) connections to the SAM to Administrators helps protect those credentials.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-002235**: Prevent non-privileged users from executing privileged functions.  
  Rev 5: AC-6 (10) · Rev 4: AC-6 (10) · Rev 3: n/a

### V-254434 · WN22-MS-000070 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 Access this computer from the network user right must only be assigned to the Administrators and Authenticated Users groups on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254434r1137691_rule` |
| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment |
| CCI | CCI-000213 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Access this computer from the network user right must only be assigned to the Administrators and Authenticated Users groups on domain-joined member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Access this computer from the network | Only: Administrators, Authenticated Users |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet; Select-String -Path "$env:TEMP\secpol.inf" -Pattern '^SeNetworkLogonRight\b'
```

Expected: SeNetworkLogonRight lists only: Administrators, Authenticated Users. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
secedit /export /cfg %TEMP%\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS /quiet && findstr /i /b "SeNetworkLogonRight" %TEMP%\secpol.inf
```

Expected: SeNetworkLogonRight lists only: Administrators, Authenticated Users. Accounts appear as names or SIDs (*S-1-5-32-544 = Administrators, *S-1-5-32-546 = Guests, *S-1-5-11 = Authenticated Users, *S-1-5-113 = Local account). No line at all means no one holds the right. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems. A separate version applies to domain controllers.

Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If any accounts or groups other than the following are granted the "Access this computer from the network" user right, this is a finding:

- Administrators
- Authenticated Users

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If any SIDs other than the following are granted the "SeNetworkLogonRight" user right, this is a finding:

S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators)
S-1-5-11 (Authenticated Users)

If an application requires this user right, this would not be a finding.

Vendor documentation must support the requirement for having the user right.

The requirement must be documented with the Information System Security Officer (ISSO).

The application account must meet requirements for application account passwords, such as length (WN22-00-000050) and required frequency of changes (WN22-00-000060).
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Access this computer from the network to include only the following accounts or groups:

- Administrators
- Authenticated Users
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

Accounts with the "Access this computer from the network" user right may access resources on the system, and this right must be limited to those requiring it.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

### V-254435 · WN22-MS-000080 · CAT II: Windows Server 2022 Deny access to this computer from the network user right on domain-joined member servers must be configured to prevent access from highly privileged domain accounts and local accounts and from unauthenticated access on all systems.

|---|---|

| Severity | CAT II (medium) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000080-GPOS-00048 |
| Topic | Windows User Rights Assignment, Account Lifecycle Management |

| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | AC-3 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | AC-3 |
| Implemented via | Group Policy |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer's Deny access to this computer from the network user right on domain-joined member servers must be configured to prevent access from highly privileged domain accounts and local accounts and from unauthenticated access on all systems.

**Why it matters:** Windows has a list of special powers, such as "shut down the computer", "look inside other programs' memory" or "log in remotely", and decides which accounts get each one. This rule makes sure only the right people, usually administrators, hold the powerful ones. It's like a hospital where only surgeons are allowed into the operating room.

**How important is it?** Medium priority (CAT II): If this setting is wrong, it could help an attacker gain access, cause damage, or hide what they did. Most rules fall into this category.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment | Deny access | Only: Enterprise Admins group, Domain Admins group |

**Command-line validation:**

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
gpresult /scope computer /h "%TEMP%\gpresult.html" /f && start "" "%TEMP%\gpresult.html"
```

Expected: Find "Deny access" in the report: it must be Only: Enterprise Admins group, Domain Admins group. Run elevated.

**How it works:** Configured at Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment. These are not registry values: they are stored in the local security database and applied from GptTmpl.inf in a GPO. Review the effective assignment with 'secedit /export /cfg c:\temp\secpol.inf /areas USER_RIGHTS' or the Local Security Policy console. An empty but defined setting means 'no one'.

**Also related (Account Lifecycle Management):** On Windows, use 'Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 35' for domain accounts. For local accounts, review 'Get-LocalUser' (LastLogon, PasswordExpires) and disable or delete accounts that aren't needed. Shared accounts require ISSO-documented justification.

**Operational impact:** Removing service accounts from rights such as 'Log on as a service' or 'Impersonate a client after authentication' can stop applications (SQL Server, IIS app pools, backup agents). Document required application accounts as approved exceptions before enforcing.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
This applies to member servers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems. A separate version applies to domain controllers.

Verify the effective setting in Local Group Policy Editor.

Run "gpedit.msc".

Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If the following accounts or groups are not defined for the "Deny access to this computer from the network" user right, this is a finding:

Domain Systems Only:
- Enterprise Admins group
- Domain Admins group
- "Local account and member of Administrators group" or "Local account" (see Note below)

All Systems:
- Guests group

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If the following SIDs are not defined for the "SeDenyNetworkLogonRight" user right, this is a finding.

Domain Systems Only:
S-1-5-root domain-519 (Enterprise Admins)
S-1-5-domain-512 (Domain Admins)
S-1-5-114 ("Local account and member of Administrators group") or S-1-5-113 ("Local account")

All Systems:
S-1-5-32-546 (Guests)

Note: These are built-in security groups. "Local account" is more restrictive but may cause issues on servers such as systems that provide failover clustering.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Deny access to this computer from the network to include the following:

Domain Systems Only:
- Enterprise Admins group
- Domain Admins group
- "Local account and member of Administrators group" or "Local account" (see Note below)

All Systems:
- Guests group

Note: These are built-in security groups. "Local account" is more restrictive but may cause issues on servers such as systems that provide failover clustering.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Deny access to this computer from the network" user right defines the accounts that are prevented from logging on from the network.

In an Active Directory Domain, denying logons to the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups on lower-trust systems helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation from credential theft attacks, which could lead to the compromise of an entire domain.

Local accounts on domain-joined systems must also be assigned this right to decrease the risk of lateral movement resulting from credential theft attacks.

The Guests group must be assigned this right to prevent unauthenticated access.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1136 Create Account; T1098 Account Manipulation

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000213**: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.  
  Rev 5: AC-3 · Rev 4: AC-3 · Rev 3: AC-3

```text
Navigate to Local Computer Policy >> Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment.

If the following accounts or groups are not defined for the "Deny log on as a service" user right on domain-joined systems, this is a finding:

- Enterprise Admins Group
- Domain Admins Group

If any accounts or groups are defined for the "Deny log on as a service" user right on nondomain-joined systems, this is a finding.

For server core installations, run the following command:

Secedit /Export /Areas User_Rights /cfg c:\path\filename.txt

Review the text file.

If the following SIDs are not defined for the "SeDenyServiceLogonRight" user right on domain-joined systems, this is a finding:

S-1-5-root domain-519 (Enterprise Admins)
S-1-5-domain-512 (Domain Admins)

If any SIDs are defined for the user right on nondomain-joined systems, this is a finding.
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Windows Settings >> Security Settings >> Local Policies >> User Rights Assignment >> Deny log on as a service to include the following:

Domain systems:
- Enterprise Admins Group
- Domain Admins Group
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Inappropriate granting of user rights can provide system, administrative, and other high-level capabilities.

The "Deny log on as a service" user right defines accounts that are denied logon as a service.

In an Active Directory Domain, denying logons to the Enterprise Admins and Domain Admins groups on lower-trust systems helps mitigate the risk of privilege escalation from credential theft attacks, which could lead to the compromise of an entire domain.

Incorrect configurations could prevent services from starting and result in a denial of service.

**Threat & control context:** User rights (privileges) such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege and SeLoadDriverPrivilege each give a direct path to SYSTEM-level compromise or credential theft. Logon rights (network, interactive, RDP, batch, service) define which accounts can authenticate through which channel. Enforcing least privilege here implements AC-6 / AC-6(10) and limits blast radius when a lower-privileged account is compromised. Pay particular attention to 'Deny' rights for privileged domain accounts on lower-tier systems, which enforce an administrative tiering model.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1134 Access Token Manipulation; T1003 OS Credential Dumping; T1078 Valid Accounts; T1003.006 OS Credential Dumping: DCSync; T1484 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle

**Severity rationale:** CAT II: any vulnerability whose exploitation has a potential to result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

### V-254441 · WN22-MS-000140 · CAT I: Windows Server 2022 must be running Credential Guard on domain-joined member servers.

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Rule ID | `SV-254441r1260031_rule` |
| Severity | CAT I (high) |
| SRG | SRG-OS-000480-GPOS-00227 |
| Topic | Windows Authentication Protocols (NTLM, Kerberos, LSA), System Services & Daemons |
| CCI | CCI-000366 |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 4 | CM-6 b |
| NIST 800-53 Rev 3 | CM-6 b |
| Implemented via | Group Policy, Registry value |
| Server role | Member server only |

#### Level 3: General Audience

**In plain terms:** This computer must be running Credential Guard on domain-joined member servers.

**Why it matters:** When you log into a Windows network, your computer and the server trade secret "handshakes" to prove who you are. Older handshakes are easy for attackers to fake or steal. This rule switches off the old, weak handshakes and protects the part of memory where Windows keeps your sign-in secrets, like retiring an old ID badge design that was easy to forge.

**How important is it?** High priority (CAT I): If this setting is wrong, an attacker could directly and immediately gain access, take control, or cause serious damage. These are fixed first.

**Key terms:**
- *UEFI / Secure Boot*: Modern computer firmware and its feature that only lets trusted software start the computer.
- *LSA / LSASS*: The Windows component that handles sign-ins and holds sign-in secrets in memory.

#### Level 2: System Administrator

**Settings changed:**

| Type | Location | Setting | Required value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registry | HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard | LsaCfgFlags | REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock) |
| Group Policy | Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard | Turn On Virtualization Based Security | "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" selected for "Credential Guard Configuration" |

**Command-line validation:**

*PowerShell* (from DISA check text)

```text
Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard
```

Expected: Compare the output with the check procedure.

*PowerShell* (generated from the setting)

```text
Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard' -Name 'LsaCfgFlags' | Select-Object -ExpandProperty 'LsaCfgFlags'
```

Expected: LsaCfgFlags = REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock). A missing value or path is a finding.

*CMD* (generated from the setting)

```text
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard" /v "LsaCfgFlags"
```

Expected: LsaCfgFlags = REG_DWORD = 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock). A missing value or path is a finding.

**How it works:** Most of these are Security Options under Local Policies, plus MS Security Guide templates (SecGuide.admx shipped with the STIG GPO package). Key settings include 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' (LmCompatibilityLevel = 5), 'Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos', 'Minimum session security for NTLM SSP', WDigest 'UseLogonCredential' = 0, and Credential Guard via Device Guard >> 'Turn On Virtualization Based Security'. Verify with 'gpresult /h' or the registry paths shown in the check.

**Also related (System Services & Daemons):** On Windows, set the service startup type through Group Policy (System Services) or 'Set-Service -StartupType Disabled'. Check with 'Get-Service <name> | Select Status, StartType'.

**Operational impact:** Enforcing NTLMv2-only or AES-only Kerberos can break legacy appliances, older NAS devices, multifunction printers and non-Windows clients. Run NTLM and Kerberos auditing (event IDs 4624/4776/4768/4769) first to inventory dependencies. Credential Guard is incompatible with some VPN clients and with unconstrained delegation.

**Check procedure (DISA):**

```text
For domain controllers and standalone or nondomain-joined systems, this is NA.
If the system is being used as an Exchange server, this requirement is not applicable.

Open "PowerShell" with elevated privileges (run as administrator).

Enter the following:

"Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_DeviceGuard -Namespace root\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard"

If "SecurityServicesRunning" does not include a value of "1" (e.g., "{1, 2}"), this is a finding.

Alternately:

Run "System Information".

Under "System Summary", verify the following:

If "Device Guard Security Services Running" does not list "Credential Guard", this is a finding.

The policy settings referenced in the Fix section will configure the following registry value. However, due to hardware requirements, the registry value alone does not ensure proper function.

Registry Hive: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE
Registry Path: \SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\DeviceGuard\

Value Name: LsaCfgFlags
Value Type: REG_DWORD
Value: 0x00000001 (1) (Enabled with UEFI lock)

A Microsoft article on Credential Guard system requirement can be found at the following link:

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/credential-guard/credential-guard-requirements
```

**Fix procedure (DISA):**

```text
Configure the policy value for Computer Configuration >> Administrative Templates >> System >> Device Guard >> Turn On Virtualization Based Security to "Enabled" with "Enabled with UEFI lock" selected for "Credential Guard Configuration".

A Microsoft article on Credential Guard system requirement can be found at the following link:

https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/identity-protection/credential-guard/credential-guard-requirements

Severity Override Guidance: The AO can allow the severity override if they have reviewed the overall protection provided to the affected servers that are not capable of complying with the Credential Guard requirement. Items that must be reviewed/considered for compliance or mitigation for non-Credential Guard compliance are:

The use of Microsoft Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) or similar products to control different local administrative passwords for all affected servers. This is to include a strict password change requirement (180 days or less).
....
Strict separation of roles and duties. Server administrator credentials cannot be used on Windows 10 desktop to administer it. Documentation of all exceptions must be supplied.
....
Use of a Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) and adherence to the Clean Source principle for administering affected servers.
....
Boundary Protection that is currently in place to protect from vulnerabilities in the network/servers.
....
Windows Defender rule block credential stealing from LSASS.exe is applied. This rule can only be applied if Windows Defender is in use.
....
The overall number of vulnerabilities that are unmitigated on the network/servers.
```

#### Level 1: Cyber Security Professional

**Vulnerability discussion (DISA):** Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to protect data that could be used in credential theft attacks if compromised. This authentication information, which was stored in the Local Security Authority (LSA) in previous versions of Windows, is isolated from the rest of operating system and can only be accessed by privileged system software.

**Threat & control context:** Windows authentication protocols are central to most domain compromise chains. Legacy LM/NTLMv1 responses can be cracked or relayed. WDigest leaves cleartext passwords in LSASS memory. Weak Kerberos encryption types (RC4/DES) enable Kerberoasting and downgrade attacks. Credential Guard and LSA protection (RunAsPPL) isolate secrets from credential-dumping tools. These settings implement IA-2(8) (replay resistance), IA-5(1)(c), SC-8 and SC-23 (session authenticity). Validate the domain-wide impact with NTLM auditing before enforcing restrictions.

**MITRE ATT&CK techniques mitigated/detected:** T1003.001 OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory; T1550.002 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash; T1557.001 LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay; T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets; T1543 Create or Modify System Process; T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

**Severity rationale:** CAT I: any vulnerability whose exploitation will directly and immediately result in loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity.

**Compliance mapping:**

- **CCI-000366**: Implement the security configuration settings.  
  Rev 5: CM-6 b · Rev 4: CM-6 b · Rev 3: CM-6 b
